phy_ocrb.3.0.summary: A force is a push or a pull that always arises from an **interaction between two objects**. Newton's third law says that when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are **equal in size and opposite in direction**: an **interaction pair**. Forces can be **contact forces** (the objects touch, such as friction, drag and normal contact force) or **non-contact forces** (acting across a gap through a field, such as gravity, magnetic and electrostatic forces). Because force has both size and direction it is a **vector**, drawn as an arrow whose length shows the size and whose direction shows the direction of the force.

core.p: A single object cannot produce a force on its own. Every force is one object acting on another, so forces always come in **pairs**. When you describe a force, say which object exerts it and which object it acts on.
bullets: A force is a **push or a pull** on an object caused by its interaction with another object.
Force is measured in **newtons (N)**.
Describe forces in the form **'force of A on B'**, for example 'force of the Earth on the ball'.
If A pushes or pulls B, then B pushes or pulls A at the same moment.
Forces can change an object's speed, direction of motion or shape.

callouts.p: A pair of forces of equal size acting in opposite directions on two different interacting objects.

core.p: Newton's third law is the rule that links the two forces in every interaction. It applies whether the objects are moving or still, speeding up or not, touching or far apart.
bullets: The two forces in an interaction pair are **equal in size**.
They act in **opposite directions**.
They act on **different objects** (one on each).
They are the **same type** of force (both gravitational, both contact, both magnetic...).
They act at the **same time**: neither force comes first.

callouts.p: When two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Same size, opposite direction, different objects, same type of force.

core.p: A contact force acts only when the two objects are **touching**. Each has its own interaction partner acting on the other object.
bullets: **Normal contact force (reaction)**: a surface pushing on an object resting on or pressing against it, at right angles to the surface.
**Friction**: opposes sliding between two surfaces; acts along the surface.
**Air resistance / drag**: friction from a gas or liquid on a moving object; opposes motion through the fluid.
**Tension**: the pull in a stretched rope, string or cable.
**Upthrust**: the upward push of a fluid on an object in it.
**Thrust / push**: for example an engine, foot or hand pushing.

core.p: A non-contact force acts **across a distance**, without the objects touching. These forces act through a **field**.
bullets: **Gravitational force**: attraction between any two masses (the Earth pulls you down; you pull the Earth up equally).
**Magnetic force**: between magnets or magnetic materials; can attract or repel.
**Electrostatic (electric) force**: between charged objects; like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
Non-contact forces also obey Newton's third law: a magnet attracts a nail, and the nail attracts the magnet with an equal force.
The force usually gets weaker as the objects move further apart.

callouts.p: Weight is a non-contact (gravitational) force. Its partner is the object pulling the Earth, not the ground pushing up.

core.p: Classifying forces is a common 1 or 2 mark question. Learn the list.
bullets: Contact: friction, air resistance, drag, tension, normal contact force, upthrust, thrust.
Non-contact: gravitational (weight), magnetic, electrostatic.
Both kinds are vectors and both come in interaction pairs.

core.p: A **vector** quantity has both **size (magnitude) and direction**; a scalar has size only. Force is a vector, so a force is not fully described until you give its direction.
bullets: Draw each force as an **arrow**.
The **length** of the arrow shows the size of the force (draw to scale when asked).
The **direction** of the arrow shows the direction of the force.
Start the arrow at the point where the force acts on the object.
Label every arrow with the name of the force and its size, for example 'friction 40 N'.
The two forces in an interaction pair would be drawn with **equal length, opposite direction**, but on **different** objects' diagrams.

callouts.p: A quantity that has both size (magnitude) and direction.

core.p: The forces in an interaction pair act on **different objects**, so they can never be added together to give a resultant force on one object. To decide whether an object speeds up you only add the forces acting **on that object**.
bullets: Resultant force is found by adding all forces on **one** object.
An interaction pair has one force on each of two objects, so the two forces are in **different** sums.
That is why a horse can pull a cart forward even though the cart pulls back on the horse equally: the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward harder than the cart pulls back.
Balanced forces (from Newton's first law) are two forces on the **same** object; an interaction pair is on **two** objects.

callouts.p: Equal and opposite does not mean balanced. Balanced forces act on one object; third-law pairs act on two different objects.

core.p: A book resting on a table has two forces on it, weight down and normal contact force up. They are equal in size and opposite, but they are **not** a third-law pair, because they both act on the book and they are different types of force.
bullets: Weight: the **Earth pulls the book** down (gravitational). Partner: **book pulls the Earth** up.
Normal contact force: the **table pushes the book** up (contact). Partner: **book pushes the table** down.
Weight and normal force are equal only because the book is in equilibrium (first law), not because of the third law.
If you lean on the book, the normal force increases but the weight does not change, which proves they are not a pair.

core.h: Third law in motion: walking, swimming, rockets
core.p: Many movements only happen because you push something backwards and it pushes you forwards.
bullets: **Walking**: your foot pushes the ground backwards (friction); the ground pushes your foot forwards. On ice there is little friction, so you cannot push back and slip.
**Swimming**: hands push water backwards; water pushes the swimmer forwards.
**Rocket**: the rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards (downwards); the gases push the rocket forwards (upwards). This works in space because it does not need air.
**Car**: tyres push backwards on the road; the road pushes the car forwards.
**Jet engine / propeller**: pushes air backwards; air pushes the plane forwards.
**Recoil of a gun**: the gun pushes the bullet forwards; the bullet pushes the gun backwards.

core.p: Both objects feel the same size force, but they do not have to move the same amount. The effect depends on **mass** (link to F = ma in P4.3).
bullets: A falling apple pulls the Earth up with the same force as the Earth pulls the apple down.
The Earth's mass is enormous, so its acceleration is far too small to notice.
When a heavy and a light skater push off each other, the forces are equal but the lighter skater moves off faster.
In a car crash with a truck, both experience equal forces, but the car (smaller mass) has the larger change in velocity.

callouts.p: Same force, different mass, different acceleration: a = F / m.

core.h: How to identify an interaction pair in an exam
core.p: Use a simple sentence swap: write the force as 'A on B', then swap the objects to get its partner.
bullets: Step 1: name the force as 'force of A on B' (for example 'force of the foot on the ball').
Step 2: swap to 'force of B on A' ('force of the ball on the foot').
Step 3: state the partner is the same size, opposite direction and the same type.
If a question gives a size, the partner force has exactly the same value in newtons.
Check the two forces are on different objects; if not, it is not a pair.

callouts.p: Full marks need size AND direction AND which object it acts on, e.g. '20 N upwards on the hand'.

analogy.p: You cannot shake hands with nobody. A handshake always involves two hands, and each hand grips the other at the same moment and equally hard. Forces are the same: there is always a pair, one on each object, at the same time. Where it breaks down: in a handshake you can choose to grip harder than your partner, but in physics the two forces are always exactly equal, and non-contact forces such as gravity need no touching at all.

terms.d: A push or pull on an object resulting from its interaction with another object; measured in newtons (N).
Two forces of equal size and opposite direction, of the same type, acting on two different interacting objects.
When two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction.
A force that acts only when two objects are touching, e.g. friction, drag, tension, normal contact force.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, through a field, e.g. gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic.
The push of a surface on an object in contact with it, at right angles to the surface (also called reaction force).
A contact force that opposes sliding between two surfaces.
A contact force opposing the motion of an object through air or water.
The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
The upward contact force on an object from a fluid it is in.
The gravitational force of the Earth (or other planet) acting on an object.
The non-contact attractive force between any two masses.
The non-contact force between charged objects; like charges repel, unlike attract.
The non-contact force between magnets, or between a magnet and a magnetic material.
A quantity with both size (magnitude) and direction, e.g. force, velocity.
A quantity with size only and no direction, e.g. mass, speed.
A region in which a non-contact force acts on an object.

mistakes.w: Weight and the normal contact force are a Newton's third law pair.
mistakes.r: They both act on the same object and are different types of force; the partner of weight is the object pulling the Earth.

mistakes.w: Third-law forces cancel so nothing can move.
mistakes.r: They act on different objects, so they cannot cancel; only forces on the same object combine.

mistakes.w: The bigger object exerts the bigger force (the Earth pulls the apple harder than the apple pulls the Earth).
mistakes.r: The forces are equal; the effects differ because the masses differ.

mistakes.w: One force is the action and comes first, then the reaction.
mistakes.r: Both forces act at the same time.

mistakes.w: Gravity is a contact force because it acts on things on the ground.
mistakes.r: Gravity is a non-contact force; it acts through a field across a distance.

mistakes.w: Giving only the size of the partner force.
mistakes.r: State size, direction and the object it acts on (e.g. 500 N upwards on the person).

mistakes.w: A rocket moves by pushing against the air.
mistakes.r: The rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards and the gases push the rocket forwards; no air needed.

mistakes.w: Force is a scalar.
mistakes.r: Force is a vector: it has size and direction.

mistakes.w: Drawing force arrows of any length.
mistakes.r: Arrow length must represent the size of the force, to scale where asked.

exam.q: State Newton's third law.
model: When two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
exam.tip: Must include both equal and opposite.

exam.q: Which of these is a non-contact force: friction, tension, magnetic force, drag?
model: Magnetic force.
exam.tip: Non-contact means acts through a field.

exam.q: Explain why force is described as a vector quantity.
model: It has both size (magnitude) and direction.
exam.tip: Both parts are needed.

exam.q: A boy pulls a rope with a force of 150 N to the left. Describe the force the rope exerts on the boy.
model: To the right (opposite direction), on the boy.
exam.tip: Size and direction are separate marks.

exam.q: Give two differences between a pair of balanced forces and a Newton's third law pair.
model: Balanced forces act on the same object; a third-law pair act on different objects.
Balanced forces can be different types; a third-law pair are the same type of force.
exam.tip: Always mention which object each force acts on.

exam.q: A cup rests on a table. Its weight is 3 N. Name the force that forms an interaction pair with the weight of the cup, giving its size and direction.
model: The gravitational force of the cup on the Earth.
Upwards.
exam.tip: Not the table pushing up: that is a contact force on the cup.

exam.q: Explain, using Newton's third law, how a person is able to walk forwards.
model: The foot pushes backwards on the ground (friction).
The ground pushes forwards on the foot with an equal force.
This forward force on the person makes them move forwards.
exam.tip: Mention friction and say why ice makes walking hard for extra understanding.

exam.q: A rocket in deep space switches on its engine. Explain why it accelerates even though there is no air to push against.
model: The rocket pushes the exhaust gases backwards.
By Newton's third law the gases exert an equal and opposite force forwards on the rocket.
This is an unbalanced force on the rocket, so it accelerates; no air is needed.
exam.tip: The interaction is between rocket and gas, not rocket and air.

exam.q: When an apple falls, the Earth exerts a force on the apple and the apple exerts a force on the Earth. Explain why the apple accelerates noticeably but the Earth does not.
model: The forces are equal in size (third law).
The Earth has a much larger mass, so its acceleration (a = F/m) is tiny.
exam.tip: Link force, mass and acceleration.

exam.q: A student says: 'A horse cannot pull a cart because the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal and opposite force, so the forces cancel.' Evaluate this statement, using ideas about interaction pairs, contact and non-contact forces and forces on each object.
model: The student is wrong.
The horse on cart and cart on horse forces are a third-law interaction pair: equal and opposite.
They act on different objects, so they cannot cancel.
To find whether the horse moves, add only forces on the horse: the ground pushes the horse forwards (friction, a contact force) as the hooves push back on the ground.
If the forward push of the ground on the horse is bigger than the backward pull of the cart, the horse accelerates.
For the cart, the horse's pull forwards is bigger than friction / drag backwards, so the cart accelerates; weight (non-contact) and normal force balance vertically.
exam.tip: Level 3 answers separate the forces on the horse from the forces on the cart.

worked.q: A magnet is held near a steel paper clip and attracts it with a force of 0.2 N to the left. Describe fully the other force in this interaction pair.
steps: Name the force: force of the magnet on the clip.
Swap the objects: force of the clip on the magnet.
Opposite direction: to the right (towards the clip).
Same type: magnetic, a non-contact force.
worked.ans: The paper clip pulls the magnet with a 0.2 N magnetic (non-contact) force to the right.

worked.q: A 60 kg skater and a 40 kg skater stand on ice and push each other apart with a force of 120 N. Compare the forces and the accelerations of the two skaters.
steps: By Newton's third law each skater feels a 120 N force, in opposite directions.
Equal forces, but the lighter skater has the larger acceleration.
worked.ans: Both forces are 120 N in opposite directions; accelerations 2.0 m/s² and 3.0 m/s².

worked.q: Using a scale of 1 cm = 10 N, describe how to draw the forces on a crate pushed with 50 N to the right against 30 N of friction.
steps: Draw the crate as a box.
Push: arrow 5 cm long pointing right from the crate, labelled 'push 50 N'.
Friction: arrow 3 cm long pointing left, labelled 'friction 30 N'.
Both arrows start on the crate because both forces act on the crate.
The partners of these forces (crate on hand, crate on floor) act on other objects so are not drawn.
worked.ans: A 5 cm right arrow and a 3 cm left arrow on the crate; arrow length shows size, direction shows direction.

phy_ocrb.3.1.summary: The **weight** of an object is the **gravitational force** the Earth (or another planet) exerts on it, measured in newtons. It is calculated with **weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g)**, where on Earth g is about **10 N/kg**. **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and is the same everywhere; weight changes from place to place because g changes. Weight is directly proportional to mass, is a **vector** acting towards the centre of the planet, and is measured with a **newtonmeter**.

core.p: In everyday life people say 'I weigh 60 kilograms', but in physics that is wrong. Kilograms measure **mass**; weight is a **force** and is measured in **newtons**.
bullets: **Mass**: the amount of matter (stuff) in an object; unit **kilogram (kg)**; a **scalar**.
**Weight**: the force of gravity acting on an object; unit **newton (N)**; a **vector**, acting downwards (towards the centre of the planet).
Mass does **not change** with location: an 80 kg astronaut is 80 kg on Earth, on the Moon and in space.
Weight **does change** with location because the gravitational field strength changes.
Mass is measured with a **balance** (in kg); weight is measured with a **newtonmeter** (spring balance, in N).

callouts.p: The force acting on an object due to gravity (the gravitational force of the Earth on the object), measured in newtons.

core.p: Weight is found by multiplying mass by the gravitational field strength. This is one of the equations you must **recall** (it is not just given), so learn it in words and symbols.
bullets: **weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)**
Rearranged: **m = W / g** and **g = W / m**.
Mass must be in **kilograms**: convert grams by dividing by 1000 (250 g = 0.25 kg).
On Earth take **g = 10 N/kg**, so the weight in newtons is ten times the mass in kilograms.

callouts.p: weight = mass × gravitational field strength, W = m g
Using grams gives an answer 1000 times too big. Always convert to kg first.

core.p: Every object with mass is surrounded by a **gravitational field**, a region where other masses feel a force. The **gravitational field strength** tells you how big the force is on each kilogram.
bullets: **g = force per kilogram** = weight / mass, unit **N/kg**.
On the Earth's surface g is about **10 N/kg** (more precisely about 9.8 N/kg): every kilogram is pulled down with about 10 N.
g depends on the **mass of the planet** (more mass, stronger field) and on how far you are from its centre (further away, weaker field).
On the Moon g is about **1.6 N/kg**, roughly one sixth of Earth's, because the Moon has much less mass.
Larger planets such as Jupiter have a stronger field (about 25 N/kg) so the same mass has a much larger weight there.
g is also the **acceleration of free fall** (about 10 m/s² on Earth): N/kg and m/s² are equivalent units.

callouts.p: The force per unit mass acting on an object in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg.

core.h: Weight is directly proportional to mass
core.p: Because g is constant in one place, doubling the mass doubles the weight. A graph of weight against mass is a **straight line through the origin**, and its **gradient equals g**.
bullets: W is **directly proportional** to m (W ∝ m) at a given location.
Gradient of W against m graph = change in W / change in m = g.
A steeper line would mean a stronger gravitational field (for example on Jupiter).
On the Moon the line would be much shallower (gradient 1.6 N/kg).

callouts.p: If asked for g from a graph, pick two points far apart on the line, not data points, and calculate rise / run with units N/kg.

core.p: A newtonmeter (spring balance) contains a spring that stretches when a load hangs from it. The extension is proportional to the force (within the limit of proportionality), so the scale can be marked directly in newtons.
bullets: Hang the object from the hook and let it come to rest.
Read the pointer at **eye level** to avoid parallax error.
Check the newtonmeter reads **zero** with nothing on it (zero error) and adjust if needed.
Choose a newtonmeter with a suitable range: a 0 to 10 N meter for small masses gives better resolution than a 0 to 100 N one.
To investigate W against m: hang increasing masses (for example 100 g slotted masses), record weight each time, then plot a graph.

core.h: Weight as a non-contact vector force
core.p: Weight is a **non-contact force**: the Earth pulls the object through its gravitational field without touching it. Because it has a direction it is a **vector** and is drawn as an arrow.
bullets: Weight acts **vertically downwards**, towards the centre of the Earth.
On a force diagram draw weight as a single arrow from the **centre of mass** of the object.
The centre of mass is the point where the whole weight of the object can be considered to act.
Arrow length shows the size of the weight; label it 'weight' and give its value in N.
Weight has an interaction partner: the object pulls the Earth upwards with an equal gravitational force (Newton's third law).

callouts.p: The normal contact force from the floor is not the third-law partner of weight. The partner is the object's gravitational pull on the Earth.

core.h: Weight on other planets and the Moon
core.p: Questions often give a different value of g. The method is identical: multiply mass by that planet's g.
bullets: An 80 kg astronaut on Earth: W = 80 × 10 = 800 N.
Same astronaut on the Moon: W = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N, about one sixth.
The astronaut's mass is still 80 kg, so it is just as hard to start them moving sideways (same inertia), even though they feel lighter.
Astronauts can jump higher on the Moon because the downward force on them is smaller.
Far out in space, far from any planet or star, g is close to zero, so weight is almost zero but mass is unchanged.

core.p: A clear layout earns method marks even if you slip on the arithmetic.
bullets: Write the equation in symbols: W = m × g.
Convert units: g to kg, tonnes to kg (1 tonne = 1000 kg).
Substitute the numbers with units.
Rearrange if needed before calculating.
Give the answer with the correct unit (N for weight, kg for mass, N/kg for g) and sensible significant figures.

callouts.p: On Earth, weight in N is about 10 times the mass in kg. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 10 N; an apple about 1 N.

core.h: Why weight matters: links to motion
core.p: Weight is the force that makes objects fall, and it appears in many later topics.
bullets: In free fall with no air resistance, weight is the only force, so acceleration = W / m = g, the same for all masses (about 10 m/s²).
Heavier objects have bigger weight, but also bigger mass, so they accelerate at the same rate: W / m = g for all.
Weight is used to find gravitational potential energy: GPE = m × g × h.
For a falling object, weight is balanced by air resistance at terminal velocity.

core.p: OCR questions often set weight in real situations. Practise recognising what is given.
bullets: Lifting loads: a crane lifts a 2 tonne load; find the weight (20 000 N) and so the minimum lifting force.
Space: compare the weight of a rover on Earth and Mars.
Practical data: a table of masses and newtonmeter readings; calculate g and comment on errors.
Free-body diagrams: draw and label weight acting from the centre of mass.
Explaining why bathroom scales 'in kg' really measure the force on them and divide by g.

callouts.p: Bathroom scales measure the force you push on them, then divide by 10 to display kg. On the Moon they would wrongly show a smaller mass.

analogy.p: Think of mass as the number of tins in your shopping bag, and gravitational field strength as how hard each tin is pulled down. The weight you feel is the number of tins multiplied by the pull on each tin. Take the same bag to the Moon and you still have the same number of tins (same mass), but each tin is pulled less (smaller g), so the bag feels lighter (smaller weight). Where it breaks down: tins are separate items, but mass is not counted in whole pieces, and the pull of gravity acts on every bit of matter at once, not on each tin individually.

terms.d: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); a scalar that does not depend on location.
The gravitational force acting on an object, measured in newtons (N); a vector acting towards the centre of the planet.
The force per kilogram acting on a mass in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg; about 10 N/kg on Earth.
A region around a mass in which another mass experiences a force.
The unit of force.
The unit of mass.
Unit of gravitational field strength: newtons per kilogram, equivalent to m/s².
A spring balance that measures force (such as weight) in newtons.
An instrument that measures mass, for example a top-pan balance.
The point at which the weight of an object can be considered to act.
Two quantities are directly proportional when doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A force that acts without objects touching, through a field; weight is an example.
A quantity with both size and direction, such as weight.
A quantity with size only, such as mass.

mistakes.w: Weight is measured in kilograms.
mistakes.r: Weight is a force measured in newtons; mass is in kilograms.

mistakes.w: On the Moon an astronaut has less mass.
mistakes.r: The mass is the same; the weight is less because g is smaller.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams in W = m g.
mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms first: 500 g = 0.5 kg.

mistakes.w: g = 10 N (or 10 kg).
mistakes.r: g = 10 N/kg.

mistakes.w: In space there is no gravity so objects have no mass.
mistakes.r: g is very small far from planets so weight is near zero, but mass is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Weight is the same everywhere.
mistakes.r: Weight depends on gravitational field strength, which varies between planets and with height.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster (with no air resistance).
mistakes.r: Acceleration = W / m = g for every object, so all fall with the same acceleration.

mistakes.w: Writing W = m / g or g = m / W.
mistakes.r: W = m × g, so g = W / m and m = W / g.

mistakes.w: Drawing the weight arrow from the bottom of the object or upwards.
mistakes.r: Draw it vertically downwards from the centre of mass.

exam.q: State the unit of gravitational field strength.
model: N/kg (newtons per kilogram).
exam.tip: m/s² is also accepted in most mark schemes, but N/kg is expected.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
model: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m g).
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both earn the mark.

exam.q: Calculate the weight of a 65 kg student on Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
exam.tip: Unit needed for the second mark.

exam.q: An apple has a weight of 1.5 N on Earth. Calculate its mass. (g = 10 N/kg)
exam.tip: Rearrange first.

exam.q: A rover has a weight of 3700 N on Mars, where g = 3.7 N/kg. Calculate its weight on Earth.
model: W on Earth = 1000 × 10
exam.tip: Two steps: find the mass, which is the same everywhere, then the new weight.

exam.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight.
model: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg, and does not change with location.
Weight is the gravitational force on the object, measured in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength.
exam.tip: Give a feature of each, with units.

exam.q: Explain why an astronaut weighs less on the Moon than on Earth, even though her mass is unchanged.
model: The gravitational field strength on the Moon is smaller (about 1.6 N/kg) because the Moon has less mass.
W = m × g, so with the same mass, smaller g gives a smaller weight.
exam.tip: Mention g and the equation.

exam.q: A student hangs masses from a newtonmeter and plots weight against mass. Describe the shape of the graph and explain how she can find g from it.
model: Straight line through the origin (directly proportional).
Calculate the gradient (change in weight / change in mass).
The gradient equals g, in N/kg.
exam.tip: Say 'gradient' explicitly.

exam.q: Suggest two ways the student could make her measurements of weight more accurate.
model: Check / correct for zero error on the newtonmeter before each reading.
Read the scale at eye level to avoid parallax / use a newtonmeter with a smaller range for better resolution / repeat and average.
exam.tip: Any two sensible, specific improvements.

exam.q: A space probe of mass 500 kg travels from Earth to Jupiter (g = 25 N/kg). Describe and explain how its mass and weight change during the journey. Include calculations of the weight on the surface of each planet.
model: Mass stays 500 kg throughout because the amount of matter does not change.
Weight on Earth = 500 × 10 = 5000 N.
As it moves away from Earth, g decreases so weight decreases.
Far from both planets g is close to zero, so weight is close to zero.
Approaching Jupiter g increases, so weight increases.
Weight on Jupiter = 500 × 25 = 12 500 N, 2.5 times its Earth weight.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs both calculations and an explanation of the change along the journey.

worked.q: A bag of potatoes has a mass of 2500 g. Calculate its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: Convert mass to kg: 2500 g / 1000 = 2.5 kg.

worked.q: An astronaut and her suit have a weight of 1200 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). Find (a) her mass and (b) her weight on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg).
steps: (b) Mass is the same on the Moon: 120 kg.

worked.q: On an unknown planet, a 4.0 kg mass hangs on a newtonmeter which reads 34.8 N. Calculate g on the planet and compare it with Earth's.
steps: Compare: 8.7 / 10 = 0.87, so objects weigh about 87% of their Earth weight there.
worked.ans: g = 8.7 N/kg, slightly less than on Earth.

phy_ocrb.3.10.summary: You can estimate stopping distances, accelerations and forces for road vehicles using typical values (car mass about 1000 to 1500 kg, speeds of about 13 m/s in towns and 31 m/s on motorways, reaction time about 0.7 s, braking deceleration about 7 m/s²). Thinking distance = speed × reaction time, braking distance can be found from v² − u² = 2as or from braking force × distance = ½mv², and forces from F = ma or change in momentum ÷ time. These estimates show that braking distance rises with speed squared and that collisions produce decelerations of hundreds of m/s² and very large forces on the body.

core.p: Engineers, road planners and examiners often need a **rough value** rather than an exact answer. Estimating uses sensible typical values and simple physics equations to get an answer to the right **order of magnitude**.
bullets: Choose sensible values for mass, speed, time or distance.
Use one or two significant figures; the answer is only approximate.
Check the answer is realistic (a car's braking deceleration is a few m/s², not thousands).
State your assumptions, for example constant deceleration.
Order of magnitude: the power of ten, e.g. 10 m/s², 100 m/s² or 1000 m/s².

callouts.p: In an estimate question, write down the values you are assuming. Any sensible value earns the marks if the method is correct.

core.p: To estimate you need a bank of realistic values for road vehicles and people.
bullets: Mass of a car: about **1000 to 1500 kg**; a lorry or bus: about **10 000 to 40 000 kg**.
Mass of a person: about **70 kg**.
Town speed (30 mph): about **13 m/s**; motorway speed (70 mph): about **31 m/s**.
Driver reaction time: **0.2 to 0.9 s**, typically about 0.7 s.
Car braking deceleration on a dry road: roughly **5 to 8 m/s²**; on ice much less.
Collision deceleration: often **hundreds of m/s²**.

callouts.p: 1 mph ≈ 0.45 m/s, so 30 mph ≈ 13 m/s and 70 mph ≈ 31 m/s.

core.p: Estimating stopping distances, accelerations and forces links several equations from P4.
bullets: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time.
Acceleration: a = (v − u) ÷ t.
Motion with constant acceleration: v² − u² = 2 × a × s.
Resultant force = mass × acceleration, F = m × a.
Work done = force × distance, and kinetic energy = ½ × m × v².
Force = change in momentum ÷ time.

head: To estimate
Use
rows: v² − u² = 2as or F × d = ½mv²
a = Δv ÷ t or a = v² ÷ 2s
F = m × a or F = Δ(mv) ÷ t

core.p: During the reaction time the car moves at constant speed, so thinking distance is easy to estimate.
bullets: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time.
A distracted driver with a 1.5 s reaction time at 31 m/s travels about 47 m before braking.
Thinking distance is **proportional to speed**.

core.p: If the braking force is constant, the deceleration is constant and you can use v² − u² = 2as with final speed v = 0.
bullets: Rearranged: braking distance s = u² ÷ (2a), using the size of the deceleration.
At 13 m/s with 7 m/s²: s = 169 ÷ 14 ≈ 12 m.
At 31 m/s with 7 m/s²: s = 961 ÷ 14 ≈ 69 m.
Braking distance is **proportional to speed squared** for a fixed deceleration.
Halving the deceleration (e.g. on a wet road) **doubles** the braking distance.

callouts.p: With v = 0, v² − u² is negative, so a is negative (a deceleration). Use the size of the deceleration when calculating a distance.

core.p: Once you know the deceleration you can estimate the braking force with F = ma, or use the work done by the brakes.
bullets: F = m × a: a 1200 kg car decelerating at 7 m/s² needs about 8400 N.
Energy method: braking force × braking distance = kinetic energy lost.
So F = ½mv² ÷ d.
A heavier vehicle at the same speed needs a **larger force** or a **longer distance** to stop.
There is a limit to the braking force: too large and the tyres lose grip and skid.

core.p: Work done by the braking force transfers energy from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings.
bullets: Work done by brakes = kinetic energy of car before braking.
Kinetic energy = ½mv², so it depends on **speed squared**.
Doubling speed means **four times** the energy, so four times the braking distance for the same force.
The brake discs and pads get **hot**; energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
Electric and hybrid cars use **regenerative braking** to transfer some of this energy to the battery instead.

callouts.p: Braking force × braking distance = ½ × m × v².

core.p: In a collision a car stops in a very short distance or time, so the deceleration is very large.
bullets: Car at 13 m/s hitting a wall and crumpling 0.5 m: a = u² ÷ 2s = 169 ÷ 1 ≈ 170 m/s².
That is about **17 times g** (g ≈ 10 m/s²).
Without a crumple zone, stopping in 0.1 m gives about 850 m/s².
Using time: stopping from 13 m/s in 0.1 s gives a = 130 m/s².
Decelerations of more than a few tens of g are likely to cause serious injury.

core.p: The force on a person in a crash is their mass times their deceleration, or their change in momentum divided by the stopping time.
bullets: A 70 kg passenger at 13 m/s stopping in 0.1 s: F = (70 × 13) ÷ 0.1 ≈ 9100 N.
This is over **13 times the passenger's weight** (about 700 N).
Air bags and seat belts increase the time so the force is much smaller.
Increasing the stopping time by 10 times reduces the force by 10 times.
Large forces on the body cause injuries such as whiplash, broken bones and head injuries.

core.p: Estimates show why some vehicles and conditions are much more dangerous than others.
bullets: A lorry has about 10 times the mass of a car, so at the same speed it has 10 times the kinetic energy.
With a similar braking force per kilogram it can stop in a similar distance, but needs a far larger total braking force.
On an icy road the deceleration may be only about 1 m/s², so braking distance at 13 m/s is about 85 m.
Wet roads roughly halve the maximum deceleration, doubling braking distance.
Speed has the biggest effect, because braking distance depends on v².

core.p: Good answers comment on how realistic the estimate is and what has been assumed.
bullets: Assumptions: constant deceleration, constant reaction time, level road, no skidding.
Real braking is not perfectly uniform, so actual distances can differ.
Compare with Highway Code values (e.g. 96 m total at 70 mph) to check your answer is sensible.
Give answers to 1 or 2 significant figures.
If an estimate gives a deceleration of thousands of m/s² for normal braking, check your working.

analogy.p: Estimating is like planning a holiday budget: you do not know the exact price of every meal, but using typical prices you can tell whether the trip will cost hundreds or thousands of pounds. In the same way, typical masses, speeds and reaction times tell you whether a car needs 10 m or 100 m to stop, and whether a crash force is hundreds or tens of thousands of newtons. Where it breaks down: a budget mistake costs money, but road safety estimates must allow for worst cases such as wet roads, tired drivers and heavy loads, so real designs build in large safety margins.

terms.d: An approximate value calculated from sensible typical values and stated assumptions.
The power of ten nearest to a value, e.g. 10, 100 or 1000.
A realistic value used in estimation, such as 1200 kg for a car or 0.7 s for a reaction time.
Distance travelled during the reaction time; speed × reaction time.
Distance travelled after the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops.
Thinking distance + braking distance.
Rate of decrease of velocity, in m/s².
Deceleration at a constant rate, allowing v² − u² = 2as to be used.
The friction force that decelerates a vehicle; braking force × braking distance = kinetic energy lost.
Energy in the kinetic store of a moving object, ½ × m × v², in joules.
Energy transferred by a force moving through a distance: force × distance.
Mass × velocity; force = change in momentum ÷ time.
About 10 N/kg; used to compare decelerations with 'g'.
Braking that transfers some kinetic energy to a battery instead of wasting it as heat.

mistakes.w: Using mph directly in equations.
mistakes.r: Convert to m/s first (30 mph ≈ 13 m/s).

mistakes.w: Braking distance = speed × reaction time.
mistakes.r: That is thinking distance; braking distance uses v² − u² = 2as or F × d = ½mv².

mistakes.w: Forgetting to square the speed in v² − u² = 2as or ½mv².
mistakes.r: Square the speed: braking distance ∝ v².

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles braking distance.
mistakes.r: Doubling speed makes braking distance four times longer at the same deceleration.

mistakes.w: Choosing unrealistic values, e.g. a car mass of 100 kg or a reaction time of 5 s.
mistakes.r: Use typical values: car about 1000–1500 kg, reaction time 0.2–0.9 s.

mistakes.w: Giving an estimate to 6 significant figures.
mistakes.r: Estimates should be given to 1 or 2 significant figures.

mistakes.w: Using the driving force in F = ma during braking.
mistakes.r: Use the resultant (braking) force that causes the deceleration.

mistakes.w: A negative braking distance from v² − u² = 2as.
mistakes.r: Use a negative acceleration for deceleration, so the distance comes out positive.

exam.q: Estimate the speed of a car travelling in a town, in m/s.
model: About 13 m/s (accept 10–15 m/s)
exam.tip: Know typical speeds in m/s.

exam.q: Estimate the thinking distance for a driver travelling at 31 m/s with a typical reaction time.
model: Reaction time about 0.7 s (accept 0.2–0.9 s)
Thinking distance = 31 × 0.7 ≈ 22 m
exam.tip: State the reaction time you assumed.

exam.q: A car travelling at 20 m/s decelerates uniformly at 5.0 m/s². Calculate its braking distance.
model: v² − u² = 2as, with v = 0
exam.tip: Use a negative acceleration for deceleration.

exam.q: The car in the question above has a mass of 1200 kg. Calculate the braking force.
exam.tip: Use the size of the deceleration.

exam.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 30 m/s stops in a braking distance of 75 m. Use energy ideas to calculate the average braking force.
model: Kinetic energy = ½ × 1500 × 30² = 675 000 J
Work done = F × d, so F = 675 000 ÷ 75
exam.tip: Kinetic energy lost = work done by brakes.

exam.q: Explain why braking distance increases by a factor of four when the speed of a car doubles, assuming the braking force stays the same.
model: Kinetic energy = ½mv², so doubling v gives four times the kinetic energy
Work done = F × d, with the same F the distance must be four times greater
exam.tip: Use both equations in your explanation.

exam.q: Estimate the deceleration of a car that hits a wall at 13 m/s and stops in 0.1 s. Compare it with g.
model: About 13 times g (g ≈ 10 m/s²)
exam.tip: Comparing with g shows how dangerous the deceleration is.

exam.q: Estimate the force on a 70 kg passenger who is stopped from 13 m/s by an air bag in 0.15 s.
model: Change in momentum = 70 × 13 = 910 kg m/s
F = change in momentum ÷ time = 910 ÷ 0.15
≈ 6100 N (accept 6000 N)
exam.tip: Give the answer to 2 significant figures for an estimate.

exam.q: A car's deceleration on an icy road is one quarter of that on a dry road. State the effect on braking distance at the same speed.
model: Braking distance is four times longer
exam.tip: s = u² ÷ 2a, so s ∝ 1/a.

exam.q: A driver travels at 31 m/s on a motorway in the rain. Estimate the total stopping distance and explain each step and assumption.
model: Assume a reaction time of about 0.7 s
Thinking distance = 31 × 0.7 ≈ 22 m
Assume a wet-road deceleration of about 3.5 m/s² (half the dry value)
Braking distance = u² ÷ 2a = 961 ÷ 7 ≈ 140 m
Stopping distance ≈ 22 + 140 ≈ 160 m
Assumes constant deceleration and no skidding; actual value could differ, so leave a larger gap
exam.tip: State each value assumed, show each equation, and comment on assumptions.

worked.q: Estimate the stopping distance of a car travelling at 13 m/s (30 mph) in good conditions.
steps: Assume reaction time 0.7 s and deceleration 7 m/s²
Check: the Highway Code gives 23 m, so the estimate is sensible

worked.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a force of 6000 N. Estimate its braking distance using energy ideas.
steps: Kinetic energy = ½ × m × v² = ½ × 1200 × 25² = 375 000 J
Work done by brakes = kinetic energy lost

worked.q: A car travelling at 13 m/s crashes. With a crumple zone the front crumples by 0.65 m. Estimate the deceleration and the force on a 70 kg driver who is held by a seat belt and stops with the car.
steps: a ≈ −130 m/s², a deceleration of about 130 m/s² (13 g)
worked.ans: Deceleration about 130 m/s², force on the driver about 9000 N

phy_ocrb.3.2.summary: **Speed** tells you how far something travels in a given time: **speed = distance travelled / time**, measured in **m/s**. You must know **typical speeds** of everyday things (walking about 1.5 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s, cars and sound) and how to **measure speed** in the lab using rulers and stopwatches or **light gates and a data logger** (PAG3). Speed is a **scalar** (size only), while **velocity** is speed in a given direction and is a **vector**; likewise distance is a scalar and **displacement** is a vector.

core.p: Speed is the **distance travelled per unit time**. A car moving at 20 m/s covers 20 metres every second. Because objects rarely move at a constant speed, the equation usually gives the **average speed** over the whole journey.
bullets: **speed (m/s) = distance travelled (m) / time (s)**, or **v = d / t** (OCR also writes s = d / t).
Rearranged: **distance = speed × time** and **time = distance / speed**.
The SI unit is **metres per second (m/s)**; km/h and mph are also used in daily life.
**Average speed** = total distance / total time for the whole journey.
**Instantaneous speed** is the speed at one particular moment (what a speedometer shows).

callouts.p: The distance travelled per unit time; speed = distance travelled / time.
distance travelled = speed × time

core.p: On a real journey speed keeps changing: you slow at junctions and speed up on straight roads. The average speed smooths all of this out.
bullets: A train covering 120 km in 2 hours has an average speed of 60 km/h even if it stopped at stations and reached 100 km/h between them.
Instantaneous speed is found over a **very short time interval** (for example the time a short card takes to pass a light gate).
On a distance-time graph, average speed is total distance / total time; instantaneous speed is the gradient of the tangent at that point (see P4.2 graphs).
Average speed cameras time a car between two cameras a known distance apart.

core.p: OCR expects you to recall typical values. They are useful for estimation questions and to check whether an answer is sensible.
bullets: Speeds of walking, running and cycling vary with age, fitness, terrain and distance travelled.
Wind speed varies a lot: a light breeze may be about 5 m/s, a gale 20 m/s or more.
The speed of sound in air is about **330 m/s** (it depends on temperature).
Light (and all electromagnetic waves) travels at **3 × 10⁸ m/s** in a vacuum.

callouts.p: Questions like 'estimate how long it takes to walk 1 km' expect you to use 1.5 m/s: t = 1000 / 1.5, about 670 s or 11 minutes.

core.p: Many marks are lost by mixing units. Always convert to metres and seconds before using v = d / t unless the question asks otherwise.
bullets: km/h to m/s: **divide by 3.6** (because 1000 / 3600 = 1 / 3.6). Example: 72 km/h / 3.6 = 20 m/s.
m/s to km/h: **multiply by 3.6**.
1 mile is about 1600 m, so 30 mph is about 13 m/s and 70 mph about 31 m/s.
Minutes to seconds: multiply by 60.
For very large or small numbers use standard form, e.g. 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

callouts.p: A time of 2 minutes 30 seconds is 150 s, not 2.30 s or 230 s.

core.p: The basic method measures a distance and a time and divides. This is fine for slow motion such as a person walking, but human reaction time limits its accuracy.
bullets: Mark out a known distance (for example 10 m) with a **tape measure** or trundle wheel.
Time the object over that distance with a **stopwatch**.
Calculate speed = distance / time.
Human **reaction time** (about 0.2 to 0.3 s) at start and stop causes **random errors**; this matters most for short times.
Improve it by timing over a longer distance (so reaction time is a smaller fraction of the total), repeating and taking a mean, and discarding anomalies.
Using the same person to start and stop the watch can reduce, but not remove, the error.

callouts.p: Say WHY a longer distance helps: the reaction time error becomes a smaller percentage of the measured time.

core.p: A **light gate** has a beam of light shining onto a sensor. When a card on a moving trolley cuts the beam, a **data logger** (or timer) records how long the beam was blocked. This removes human reaction time.
bullets: Measure the **length of the card** (interrupt card) with a ruler.
Release the trolley down a ramp so the card passes through the light gate.
The data logger records the **time the beam is blocked**.
**Speed = length of card / time beam blocked**.
Because the time is very short, this gives close to the **instantaneous speed** at the gate.
Two light gates, or a double interrupt card, allow you to find the speed at two points and so the **acceleration** (link to P4.2 acceleration).
Light gates give more **accurate** and **precise** timings than a hand-held stopwatch, with higher resolution (e.g. to 0.001 s).

callouts.p: No human reaction time, so smaller random error, and the timer has a much better resolution.

core.p: Different situations call for different methods.
bullets: **Video analysis**: film the motion next to a scale and step through frames; the frame rate gives the time between images.
**Ticker timer**: makes dots on tape at fixed time intervals (for example 50 per second); the spacing shows the distance per interval.
**Speed cameras and radar guns**: police measure the speed of cars (some use two photos a known time apart over road markings).
**Sat nav / GPS**: calculates speed from changes in position over time.
**Speedometer**: shows instantaneous speed in a vehicle.

core.p: Physical quantities fall into two groups. A **scalar** has only a size (magnitude). A **vector** has a size **and a direction**. Vectors are drawn as arrows: the length shows the size, the arrow shows the direction.
bullets: **Scalars**: distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature, power, volume.
**Vectors**: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force (including weight), momentum.
A direction can be given as a compass bearing, an angle, 'up/down', 'left/right', or as a **+ or - sign** in one dimension.
Adding vectors must take direction into account: 3 N right plus 3 N left gives 0 N, not 6 N.

callouts.p: A scalar quantity has magnitude only; a vector quantity has magnitude and direction.

core.p: **Distance** is how far you actually travel along your path; it is a scalar. **Displacement** is how far you end up from where you started, **in a straight line, with a direction**; it is a vector.
bullets: Walk 30 m east then 40 m north: distance = 70 m, but displacement = 50 m north-east (using Pythagoras, 30² + 40² = 50²).
Run one lap of a 400 m track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 m (you finish where you started).
Displacement can never be bigger than distance; they are equal only for motion in a straight line without turning back.
Displacement can be negative in one dimension (moved back past the start).

core.p: **Velocity** is speed in a stated direction. Two objects can have the same speed but different velocities if they are moving in different directions.
bullets: **Velocity = displacement / time**, unit m/s, with a direction.
A car going round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s has a **constant speed** but a **changing velocity**, because its direction keeps changing.
In one dimension, choose one direction as positive: +20 m/s and -20 m/s mean the same speed in opposite directions.
A change in velocity (speed or direction) means the object is **accelerating** (link to P4.2 and circular motion in P4.3).
A ball thrown up and caught again has average velocity zero (zero displacement) but a non-zero average speed.

callouts.p: Speed in a given direction; the rate of change of displacement.
Constant speed does not mean constant velocity. Moving in a circle at steady speed is accelerating.

core.p: Use the same layout for every speed question.
bullets: List the data with units; convert to m and s.
Write the equation: speed = distance / time.
Rearrange if needed (distance = speed × time; time = distance / speed).
Substitute and calculate.
Give the unit and check against typical speeds: a cyclist at 600 m/s means a mistake.

analogy.p: Speed is like telling someone 'I walked for 10 minutes at a normal pace': it tells them how fast but not where. Velocity is like saying 'I walked at a normal pace towards the station': now they know how fast and which way. Distance is the length of all the twisting streets you walked; displacement is 'as the crow flies' with a direction, like the arrow on a map from your house to your friend's. Where it breaks down: in real directions the route matters for getting there, but in physics displacement ignores the route completely; and directions give a place, whereas velocity can change from moment to moment.

terms.d: Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar, unit m/s.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
The speed at a particular instant, measured over a very short time interval.
Speed in a given direction; displacement per unit time; a vector.
How far an object travels along its path; a scalar, unit m.
The straight-line distance from start to finish in a stated direction; a vector, unit m.
A quantity that has magnitude (size) only.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
The size of a quantity, ignoring direction.
A sensor with a light beam that records when an object blocks the beam, used with a data logger to measure time intervals.
Electronic device that automatically records measurements from sensors over time.
A card of known length fixed to a moving object that blocks a light gate's beam.
The time taken to respond to a stimulus; about 0.2 to 0.3 s, causing errors in hand timing.
Unpredictable scatter in repeated measurements, reduced by repeating and averaging.
The smallest change in a quantity an instrument can show.
The SI unit of speed and velocity.

mistakes.w: Speed and velocity are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Velocity is speed in a given direction; velocity is a vector, speed is a scalar.

mistakes.w: Speed = time / distance.
mistakes.r: Speed = distance / time.

mistakes.w: Using km and s (or m and h) together.
mistakes.r: Convert to m and s to get m/s (or km and h for km/h).

mistakes.w: Converting km/h to m/s by multiplying by 3.6.
mistakes.r: Divide by 3.6 to go from km/h to m/s.

mistakes.w: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is not accelerating.
mistakes.r: Its direction changes, so its velocity changes, so it is accelerating.

mistakes.w: Light gates are better because they are more reliable / easier.
mistakes.r: They remove human reaction time, giving smaller random errors and higher resolution timing.

mistakes.w: Displacement after a lap of the track is 400 m.
mistakes.r: Displacement is 0 m because the runner finishes at the start; distance is 400 m.

mistakes.w: Mass is a vector / force is a scalar.
mistakes.r: Mass is a scalar; force is a vector.

mistakes.w: Typical walking speed is 10 m/s.
mistakes.r: About 1.5 m/s; 10 m/s is close to a world-class sprinter.

exam.q: State the typical speed of a person walking.
model: About 1.5 m/s (accept 1 to 2 m/s).
exam.tip: Give units.

exam.q: Which of these is a vector quantity: distance, speed, mass, velocity?
model: Velocity.
exam.tip: Vectors have direction.

exam.q: Explain the difference between speed and velocity.
model: Speed has magnitude only / is a scalar.
Velocity has magnitude and direction / is a vector (speed in a given direction).
exam.tip: Use the words scalar and vector.

exam.q: A cyclist travels 1.8 km in 5 minutes. Calculate her average speed in m/s.
model: Convert: 1800 m and 300 s.
speed = distance / time = 1800 / 300
exam.tip: Convert both units before dividing.

exam.q: Sound travels at 330 m/s. Calculate how far away a lightning strike is if thunder is heard 4.0 s after the flash.
model: distance = speed × time = 330 × 4.0
exam.tip: The light arrives almost instantly, so the delay is the sound's travel time.

exam.q: A car travels at 108 km/h. Convert this speed into m/s.
exam.tip: Show the working for the method mark.

exam.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 80 s. State her distance and displacement, and calculate her average speed.
model: Distance = 400 m.
Displacement = 0 m.
Average speed = 400 / 80 = 5.0 m/s.
exam.tip: Her average velocity would be zero.

exam.q: A car goes round a roundabout at a constant speed. Explain why its velocity is not constant.
model: Its direction of motion is changing.
Velocity is a vector (depends on direction), so the velocity changes.
exam.tip: Link to acceleration for a stretch mark.

exam.q: A student times a toy car over 1.0 m using a stopwatch. Explain why using a light gate and data logger would give a more accurate value of speed.
model: Stopwatch timing includes human reaction time at start and stop.
This is a large fraction of a short time / causes random error.
Light gate times automatically / no reaction time and higher resolution, so more accurate.
exam.tip: Always name reaction time.

exam.q: Describe how you would use a light gate and data logger to measure the speed of a trolley at the bottom of a ramp. Include how you would calculate the speed and how you would make the result reliable.
model: Attach a card of known length to the trolley; measure its length with a ruler.
Place the light gate at the bottom of the ramp, connected to the data logger, at the height of the card.
Release the trolley from rest from a marked point so the card passes through the beam.
Data logger records the time the beam is blocked.
Speed = card length / time.
Repeat several times from the same start position, discard anomalies and calculate a mean.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs method, calculation and a reliability step.

worked.q: A train travels 240 km in 1 hour 20 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
steps: Check: 50 m/s fits a high speed train.

worked.q: A 5.0 cm card on a trolley blocks a light gate for 0.125 s. Calculate the trolley's speed.
Estimate how long it takes a student to walk 2 km to school, using a typical walking speed.

phy_ocrb.3.3.summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: acceleration = change in speed ÷ time taken, measured in m/s². It is a vector, so slowing down gives a negative acceleration (deceleration). When distance rather than time is known, the equation v² − u² = 2as links initial speed, final speed, uniform acceleration and distance. In PAG3 you measure acceleration, usually with light gates, cards and a data logger, and you must explain how to reduce errors.

core.p: **Acceleration** tells you how quickly velocity changes. It is not the same as speed: a fast car on a straight motorway at a steady 30 m/s has zero acceleration, while a slow bike pulling away from traffic lights has a large acceleration. Because velocity is a vector, acceleration is also a **vector** and has a direction.
bullets: Acceleration = **rate of change of velocity** (how much the velocity changes each second).
An acceleration of 3 m/s² means the velocity changes by **3 m/s every second**.
Speeding up, slowing down and changing direction are all changes in velocity, so all are accelerations.
Constant speed in a straight line means **zero acceleration**.
In OCR questions on straight-line motion, 'change in speed' and 'change in velocity' are used in the same way; the sign shows the direction.

callouts.p: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken for the change. It is a vector quantity measured in m/s².

core.p: The equation you must recall links acceleration, the change in speed and the time taken. Writing the change in speed as (v − u), final minus initial, makes the sign come out correctly every time.
bullets: acceleration (m/s²) = change in speed (m/s) ÷ time taken (s)
In symbols: **a = (v − u) ÷ t**, where u = initial speed and v = final speed.
Rearranged for the change in speed: (v − u) = a × t, so v = u + a × t.
Rearranged for time: t = (v − u) ÷ a.
Always do **final minus initial**: doing it the other way round gives the wrong sign.

callouts.p: acceleration = change in speed ÷ time taken. You must remember this one; it is not on the equation sheet.

core.p: The unit comes straight from the equation: a change in speed (m/s) divided by a time (s) gives (m/s) per second, written m/s² or m s⁻².
bullets: Read m/s² as 'metres per second, per second'.
It is the number of m/s gained (or lost) in each second.
Never write m/s for an acceleration: that is the unit of speed and loses the unit mark.
Convert km/h to m/s first: divide by 3.6 (for example 72 km/h = 20 m/s).
Convert minutes to seconds before using a = (v − u) ÷ t.

core.p: When an object slows down, v is smaller than u, so (v − u) is negative and the acceleration comes out negative. A negative acceleration in the direction of motion is called a **deceleration**: the acceleration points the opposite way to the velocity.
bullets: A car slowing from 20 m/s to 0 m/s in 5 s: a = (0 − 20) ÷ 5 = **−4 m/s²**.
You can say 'acceleration of −4 m/s²' or 'deceleration of 4 m/s²', but not 'deceleration of −4 m/s²'.
The minus sign shows **direction**, not 'less than nothing'.
Braking forces, friction and air resistance acting against motion cause decelerations.

callouts.p: If a question asks for the deceleration, give a positive number. Writing 'deceleration = −4 m/s²' actually means speeding up.

core.p: OCR expects you to make sensible estimates. Knowing a few typical values lets you check whether an answer is realistic: a car accelerating at 500 m/s² is clearly a calculator slip.
bullets: Free fall near the Earth's surface: about **10 m/s²** (9.8 m/s²), with negligible air resistance.
Family car pulling away: roughly 2 to 3 m/s².
Sprinter at the start of a race: roughly 3 to 5 m/s².
Car braking hard on a dry road: deceleration of roughly 6 to 8 m/s².
A crash or a hard landing can give decelerations of hundreds of m/s², because the stop happens in a tiny time.

callouts.p: OCR questions usually give g = 10 N/kg (or 10 m/s²). Use the value printed in the question.

core.h: Seeing acceleration on a velocity-time graph
core.p: On a velocity-time graph the **gradient** (slope) equals the acceleration, because gradient = change in velocity ÷ change in time, which is exactly the acceleration equation. A straight sloping line therefore means **uniform (constant) acceleration**.
bullets: Steeper line = bigger acceleration.
Line sloping down = negative acceleration (deceleration).
Horizontal line = constant velocity, zero acceleration.
A curved line means the acceleration is changing.
The full graph skills (areas, tangents) belong to the distance-time and velocity-time graphs point.

core.p: Sometimes you know the distance travelled but not the time. The equation (final speed)² − (initial speed)² = 2 × acceleration × distance links speed, acceleration and distance without needing time. It is given on the OCR equation sheet, but you must choose it and use it correctly.
bullets: (final speed (m/s))² − (initial speed (m/s))² = 2 × acceleration (m/s²) × distance (m)
In symbols: **v² − u² = 2as** (some books write 2ad).
It only works for **uniform (constant) acceleration** in a straight line.
Use it when a question gives (or asks for) a **distance** and does not mention time.
Square each speed separately: v² − u² is NOT the same as (v − u)².

callouts.p: Time given or wanted: use a = (v − u) ÷ t. Distance given or wanted with no time: use v² − u² = 2as.

core.p: Most marks are lost in the algebra, so learn the rearrangements and always write the substituted numbers before you calculate.
bullets: For acceleration: a = (v² − u²) ÷ 2s.
For distance: s = (v² − u²) ÷ 2a.
For final speed: v² = u² + 2as, then **take the square root** to get v.
For initial speed: u² = v² − 2as, then square root.
Starting from rest means **u = 0**; coming to a stop means **v = 0**.
For stopping, a is negative, so v² − u² = 2as gives −u² = 2as, and s = u² ÷ (2 × deceleration).
Stopping distance (braking part) is proportional to speed squared: double the speed, four times the braking distance.

callouts.p: When solving for v or u, the number you get from u² + 2as is the speed SQUARED. Square root it before writing the answer.

core.h: PAG3: investigating acceleration with light gates
core.p: In the practical activity group PAG3 you measure speed and acceleration. A common method is a trolley rolling down a ramp through two light gates connected to a data logger.
bullets: Fix a card of known length (for example 10 cm) on top of the trolley.
Set up a ramp at a fixed angle, with two light gates a measured distance apart.
Release the trolley from rest from the same marked point each time (do not push it).
Each gate records the time the card blocks the beam: speed = card length ÷ blocking time.
The logger also records the time taken to travel between the two gates.
Calculate a = (v − u) ÷ t, using u from gate 1, v from gate 2 and t between gates.
Or calculate a = (v² − u²) ÷ 2s, using s = distance between the gates.
Repeat at least three times and find a mean; change the independent variable (ramp angle, or the force pulling the trolley) and repeat.

core.h: Variables and fair testing in PAG3
core.p: A good plan names the variables clearly. What you change depends on the question being investigated, for example how ramp height (angle) affects acceleration, or how the accelerating force affects acceleration on a level runway.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the one you change (for example height of the raised end of the ramp).
**Dependent variable**: the one you measure (acceleration of the trolley).
**Control variables**: same trolley mass, same card, same release point, same ramp surface, same distance between gates.
Plot acceleration against the independent variable and draw a line of best fit.
If a hanging mass pulls the trolley, keep the **total** mass of the system constant by moving masses from trolley to hanger.

core.p: Light gates are not the only method. OCR may describe a different set-up and ask you to process its data.
bullets: **Ticker timer**: makes 50 dots per second on a paper tape; gaps between dots show how far the trolley moved in each 0.02 s.
**Single light gate with a double interrupter card**: two segments of known length give two speeds and the time between them.
**Stopwatch and metre rule**: time over a measured distance; simple but large timing errors from human reaction time.
**Video analysis**: film the motion against a scale and step through frames of known time interval.
**Motion sensor** (ultrasound): measures distance many times a second and plots graphs directly.

core.p: Examiners reward specific, explained improvements rather than vague ones like 'be more careful'.
bullets: Hand timing with a stopwatch has a **reaction time** of about 0.2 to 0.3 s, which is large compared with times of 1 s or less: light gates remove this **random error**.
Measure the card length precisely; an error in card length gives a **systematic error** in every speed.
Friction slows the trolley: tilting the runway slightly can compensate for friction.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors; spot and ignore anomalous results.
Make sure the card passes straight through the beam and the trolley does not wobble or hit the gate.
Increase the distance between gates so the change in speed (and the time) is larger, giving a smaller percentage uncertainty.

callouts.p: State the problem, the change, and why it helps: 'use light gates instead of a stopwatch because they remove human reaction time error'.

core.h: Calculation method that earns full marks
core.p: OCR mark schemes give marks for the equation, the substitution and the answer with unit. Showing each step protects you from losing everything for one slip.
bullets: 1. Write down the known values with units (u, v, a, s, t).
2. Convert units (km/h to m/s, cm to m, minutes to s).
3. Pick the equation: is time involved, or distance?
4. Rearrange, then substitute the numbers.
5. Calculate, take a square root if needed, and give the unit (m/s², m/s, m or s).
6. Round sensibly (usually 2 or 3 significant figures) and check that the answer is realistic.

analogy.t: Acceleration is like a savings rate
analogy.p: Think of velocity as the money in a piggy bank and acceleration as how many pounds you add each week. Adding £3 every week is like an acceleration of 3 m/s²: the total (velocity) grows steadily. Taking money out each week is a deceleration. A big total with nothing added is a high speed with zero acceleration. Where it breaks down: money has no direction, but velocity and acceleration are vectors, so turning a corner at a steady speed is still an acceleration, which the piggy bank cannot show.

terms.d: The rate of change of velocity: change in velocity divided by time taken. A vector, unit m/s².
Slowing down; an acceleration in the opposite direction to the velocity (negative acceleration).
Acceleration that stays constant, so velocity changes by the same amount every second.
The speed at the start of the time or distance being considered, in m/s.
The speed at the end of the time or distance being considered, in m/s.
Speed in a stated direction; a vector quantity.
A quantity with both size (magnitude) and direction, such as velocity, acceleration and force.
A quantity with size only, such as speed, distance and time.
Metres per second per second: the change in speed in m/s that happens each second.
The acceleration of an object falling with no air resistance, about 10 m/s² near the Earth's surface.
Change in velocity divided by change in time, equal to the acceleration.
A sensor with a beam of light; it records when an object breaks the beam and for how long.
Electronic device that records readings from sensors automatically and can calculate speeds and times.
Card of known length fixed to a trolley so that a light gate can time it and calculate speed.
The delay between an event and a person responding to it; causes random error in hand timing.
Unpredictable scatter in readings; reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts every reading by the same amount or in the same direction, such as a wrongly measured card length.

mistakes.w: Acceleration is how fast something is going.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (change in velocity ÷ time); speed is how fast it is going.

mistakes.w: Unit of acceleration written as m/s.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is measured in m/s² (metres per second per second).

mistakes.w: Using (u − v) ÷ t, giving the wrong sign.
mistakes.r: a = (v − u) ÷ t: final speed minus initial speed.

mistakes.w: Working out (v − u)² instead of v² − u².
mistakes.r: Square each speed separately and then subtract: v² − u².

mistakes.w: Giving v² as the answer when asked for v.
mistakes.r: Take the square root of v² = u² + 2as to get the speed.

mistakes.w: Using v² − u² = 2as when the acceleration is changing.
mistakes.r: The equation only applies to uniform (constant) acceleration.

mistakes.w: Deceleration = −4 m/s².
mistakes.r: Either acceleration = −4 m/s² or deceleration = 4 m/s².

mistakes.w: Improve the experiment by 'being more accurate' or 'doing it more carefully'.
mistakes.r: Name a specific change and its reason, such as using light gates to remove reaction time error, or repeating and averaging.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert km/h or cm before substituting.
mistakes.r: Convert to m/s, m and s first (km/h ÷ 3.6; cm ÷ 100).

exam.q: State the equation that links acceleration, change in speed and time taken.
model: acceleration = change in speed ÷ time taken (a = (v − u) ÷ t)
exam.tip: Words or correct symbols both score; a triangle alone does not.

exam.q: Give the unit of acceleration.
model: m/s² (or m s⁻²)
exam.tip: m/s is the unit of speed and scores zero.

exam.q: A train speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 40 s. Calculate its acceleration.
model: a = 0.5 m/s²
exam.tip: Show the substitution: it earns a mark even if the arithmetic slips.

exam.q: A car decelerates at 4 m/s² for 6 s. It started at 30 m/s. Calculate its final speed.
model: v = 6 m/s
exam.tip: Put the deceleration in as a negative acceleration.

exam.q: A stone is dropped from rest down a well and hits the water at 15 m/s. Use v² − u² = 2as and g = 10 m/s² to calculate the depth of the well.
exam.tip: Starting from rest means u = 0.

exam.q: An aircraft accelerates uniformly from rest at 3.0 m/s² along a runway 1500 m long. Calculate its speed at the end of the runway.
exam.tip: Remember the square root step.

exam.q: Explain why a car's braking distance increases by a factor of four when its speed doubles, assuming the same deceleration.
model: From v² − u² = 2as with v = 0, braking distance s = u² ÷ 2 × deceleration
s is proportional to u², so 2² = 4 times the distance
exam.tip: Link the factor of 4 to the squared speed in the equation.

exam.q: A student times a trolley rolling down a ramp with a stopwatch. Suggest one improvement and explain how it improves the results.
model: Use light gates / data logger (or repeat and calculate a mean)
Removes human reaction time error (or reduces effect of random errors)
exam.tip: Improvement plus reason: one mark each.

exam.q: Light gate 1 records a 0.10 m card blocking the beam for 0.20 s. Light gate 2 records 0.050 s. The trolley takes 0.75 s to travel between the gates. Calculate the acceleration.
model: a = 2.0 m/s²
exam.tip: Work out each speed first using speed = distance ÷ time, then use the acceleration equation.

exam.q: Describe how you would investigate how the height of a ramp affects the acceleration of a trolley rolling down it. Include how you would calculate the acceleration and how you would make the results reliable.
model: Set up ramp with two light gates a measured distance apart, connected to a data logger
Fix a card of measured length to the trolley; release from rest from the same point
Speed at each gate = card length ÷ time beam is blocked
Acceleration = (v − u) ÷ time between gates (or (v² − u²) ÷ 2s)
Change the height of the raised end (measured with a ruler); keep trolley mass, release point, gate separation the same
Repeat each height at least three times, calculate means, remove anomalies, plot acceleration against height
exam.tip: Six-mark answers are marked on levels: cover method, calculation and control/reliability in a logical order.

exam.q: A sprinter reaches 9 m/s in 2.0 s. Estimate her acceleration and comment on whether it is a typical value.
model: Typical for a sprinter start (a few m/s², less than g)
exam.tip: Comparing with free fall (10 m/s²) is a quick sense check.

worked.q: A cyclist speeds up from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. Calculate her acceleration.
steps: Known: u = 4 m/s, v = 10 m/s, t = 3 s.
Equation: acceleration = change in speed ÷ time taken, a = (v − u) ÷ t.

worked.q: A car travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 5 m/s² until it stops. Calculate the braking distance.
steps: Known: u = 25 m/s, v = 0 m/s, a = −5 m/s². No time is given, so use v² − u² = 2as.

worked.q: A ball is dropped from rest and falls 5.0 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground.
steps: Known: u = 0 m/s, a = 10 m/s², s = 5.0 m. Distance given, no time: use v² − u² = 2as.

phy_ocrb.3.4.summary: Motion graphs let you read a journey at a glance. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and on a curved line the gradient of a tangent gives the instantaneous speed. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled. Objects in free fall near the Earth accelerate at about 10 m/s² whatever their mass, until air resistance makes the acceleration fall to zero at terminal velocity.

core.p: Motion graphs turn a description of a journey into a picture you can measure. OCR expects you to draw them from data, read values from them, and translate between the graph, words and numbers. The two key types are **distance-time** and **velocity-time** graphs, and the trick is to know what the gradient and the area of each one mean.
bullets: Time always goes on the x-axis (horizontal).
Distance-time graph: **gradient = speed**.
Velocity-time graph: **gradient = acceleration**; **area under the line = distance travelled**.
A straight line means a constant gradient; a curve means the gradient (speed or acceleration) is changing.
Always read the axis labels first: confusing the two graph types is the most common mistake.

core.p: A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled from its starting point as time passes. Its shape tells you immediately whether the object is moving, stopped or changing speed.
bullets: Straight line through the origin: constant speed from the start.
**Horizontal line**: distance is not changing, so the object is **stationary**.
Steeper line: higher speed.
Line curving upwards (getting steeper): **speeding up** (accelerating).
Line curving and levelling off (getting less steep): **slowing down**.
A distance-time line can never slope downwards, because distance travelled never decreases (a displacement-time graph can).

core.h: Speed from the gradient of a distance-time graph
core.p: Gradient means 'rise over run'. On a distance-time graph the rise is a distance and the run is a time, so the gradient is distance ÷ time, which is speed.
bullets: Pick two points far apart on a straight section.
Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time.
Units: m ÷ s = **m/s**.
Example: a line rising from 0 m to 120 m between 0 s and 40 s has gradient 120 ÷ 40 = 3 m/s.
For a whole journey with stops, **average speed** = total distance ÷ total time (the gradient of a straight line from start to finish).

callouts.p: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed. Steeper means faster.

core.h: Higher tier: tangents for changing speed
core.p: When the distance-time graph is curved the speed is different at every instant. To find the **instantaneous speed** at one moment, draw a **tangent**: a straight line that just touches the curve at that point, with the same slope as the curve there. Then find the gradient of the tangent.
bullets: Place a ruler so it touches the curve at the point without cutting across it.
Extend the tangent so you can draw a **large triangle**: big triangles reduce reading errors.
Speed at that instant = Δd ÷ Δt of the tangent.
The same tangent method finds the instantaneous acceleration from a curved velocity-time graph.
Instantaneous speed can differ a lot from the average speed over the whole journey.

callouts.p: Draw the triangle on the graph and write the values you read off. Examiners award marks for the method even if your reading is slightly different.

core.p: A velocity-time graph shows how the velocity of an object changes. Because velocity is a vector, the line can go below the time axis if the object moves backwards.
bullets: Horizontal line above the axis: **constant velocity** (zero acceleration).
Horizontal line on the time axis: stationary.
Straight line sloping up: **uniform acceleration**.
Straight line sloping down: **uniform deceleration**.
Line below the time axis: moving in the opposite (negative) direction.
Curve getting less steep: acceleration decreasing (for example a falling object approaching terminal velocity).
