core.h: Acceleration from the gradient of a velocity-time graph
core.p: On a velocity-time graph the rise is a change in velocity and the run is a time, so the gradient is (change in velocity) ÷ (time taken), which is the definition of acceleration.
bullets: Acceleration = gradient = (v − u) ÷ t.
Units: (m/s) ÷ s = **m/s²**.
A negative gradient gives a negative acceleration (deceleration).
Example from the graph above: 0 to 4 s, a = (10 − 0) ÷ 4 = 2.5 m/s²; 11 to 15 s, a = (0 − 10) ÷ 4 = −2.5 m/s².
The steeper the line, the greater the size of the acceleration.

callouts.p: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.

core.h: Distance from the area under a velocity-time graph
core.p: The area between the line and the time axis is the distance travelled. This works because distance = speed × time: each thin strip under the line has height velocity and width time, so its area is a distance, and adding all the strips gives the total.
bullets: Split the area into **rectangles** (constant velocity) and **triangles** (uniform acceleration).
Rectangle area = base × height = time × velocity.
Triangle area = ½ × base × height.
Add the pieces for the total distance travelled.
Check units: s × m/s = **m**.
For a trapezium you can also use ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × width.

callouts.p: Distance on a velocity-time graph comes from the AREA, not from reading the velocity value or the gradient.

core.h: Higher tier: areas under curved lines
core.p: If the velocity-time line is curved you cannot use simple shapes exactly, so you estimate the area by **counting squares**.
bullets: Work out the distance one grid square represents: (velocity per square) × (time per square).
Count whole squares under the line, and count squares that are half or more as one; ignore smaller fragments.
Multiply the number of squares by the distance per square.
Example: each square is 2 m/s by 1 s = 2 m; 37 squares means about 74 m.
This gives an **estimate**: say so in your answer.

core.p: Many OCR questions describe a journey in words and ask you to sketch the graph, or show a graph and ask you to describe the motion. Use precise words that match the shape.
bullets: Describe each section with the right term: accelerates, constant speed, decelerates, stationary.
Quote numbers from the graph: 'accelerates uniformly from 0 to 10 m/s in 4 s'.
When sketching, label axes with quantity and unit, and use straight lines for constant gradients.
A stop on a distance-time graph is a flat line; a stop on a velocity-time graph is a line ON the time axis.
Joining up the two: the steepness of a distance-time graph matches the height of the velocity-time graph at the same time.

core.p: An object falling freely near the Earth's surface accelerates downwards because of its weight. If air resistance is negligible, **all objects fall with the same acceleration** whatever their mass: about **10 m/s²** (more precisely 9.8 m/s²). This value is the gravitational field strength g, which can be written in N/kg or m/s².
bullets: Free fall means the only force acting is weight (gravity).
A heavier object has a bigger weight but also more mass to accelerate, so a = weight ÷ mass = g is the same for all objects.
A hammer and a feather dropped on the Moon (no air) land together; the Moon's g is about 1.6 m/s².
On a velocity-time graph free fall without air resistance is a **straight line of gradient 10 m/s²**.
In air, drag increases with speed, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease; the graph curves and levels off at **terminal velocity**.
Each second of free fall from rest adds about 10 m/s: after 3 s, v is about 30 m/s.

callouts.p: Acceleration in free fall near the Earth's surface is about 10 m/s² (9.8 m/s²).

core.h: Measuring g and motion data in practicals
core.p: Data for motion graphs come from measurements of distance and time, for example in PAG3. You can also measure the acceleration due to gravity.
bullets: Drop a card or 'picket fence' through a light gate: the data logger calculates velocity at intervals and plots a velocity-time graph whose gradient is g.
Use a ticker timer with a falling mass: dot gaps increase steadily, showing uniform acceleration.
Use a dense, compact object so air resistance is small compared with weight.
Using a motion sensor, the computer can draw distance-time and velocity-time graphs directly.
Repeat and average to reduce random error; light gates avoid human reaction time.

core.p: Graph questions are often worth several marks for reading values carefully and showing working.
bullets: Read scales carefully: check what one small square represents.
Write the gradient or area calculation with values and units.
Use a ruler for tangents and lines, a sharp pencil for points.
Large triangles for gradients give more accurate answers.
Check your answer is sensible, for example a walking speed of about 1.5 m/s, not 150 m/s.

analogy.p: Imagine a distance-time graph as the profile of a hill you walk across from left to right: the steeper the climb, the faster the object is moving, and a flat plateau means it has stopped. A velocity-time graph is like a rain gauge on a car roof: the height of the line is how fast you are going and the total 'puddle' (area) collected underneath is how far you have gone. Where it breaks down: a real hill can slope down, but a distance-time graph cannot, and the 'area' only means distance when the y-axis is velocity.

terms.d: A graph of distance travelled (y-axis) against time (x-axis); its gradient is the speed.
A graph of velocity (y-axis) against time (x-axis); its gradient is the acceleration and its area is the distance travelled.
The steepness of a line: change in the y-axis quantity divided by change in the x-axis quantity.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The speed at one particular moment; the gradient of the tangent to a distance-time graph at that time.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
The distance travelled in that time interval.
Constant acceleration; shown by a straight sloping line on a velocity-time graph.
Not moving; a horizontal line on a distance-time graph or a line on the time axis of a velocity-time graph.
Same speed in the same direction; a horizontal line (above or below the axis) on a velocity-time graph.
Motion of an object falling when the only force acting on it is its weight.
The acceleration of an object in free fall, about 10 m/s² (9.8 m/s²) near the Earth's surface.
A friction force from the air that opposes motion and increases with speed.
The constant maximum velocity reached by a falling object when drag equals weight, so the resultant force is zero.
Method for estimating the area under a curved graph by counting grid squares and multiplying by the value of one square.

mistakes.w: The horizontal line on the velocity-time graph shows the object is stopped.
mistakes.r: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph is constant velocity; stationary only if the line is on the time axis (v = 0).

mistakes.w: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the speed.
mistakes.r: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration; the gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed.

mistakes.w: Distance from a velocity-time graph = velocity × time read at the end.
mistakes.r: Distance is the area under the line, adding triangles and rectangles.

mistakes.w: Using ½ × base × height for every section.
mistakes.r: Use ½ × base × height only for triangles; rectangles are base × height.

mistakes.w: Gradient found from a tiny triangle or from one point (d ÷ t at that point on a curve).
mistakes.r: Draw a tangent and use a large triangle: Δd ÷ Δt.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster.
mistakes.r: With negligible air resistance all objects have the same acceleration, g = 10 m/s².

mistakes.w: At terminal velocity there are no forces acting.
mistakes.r: Weight and drag are equal and opposite, so the resultant force (and acceleration) is zero.

mistakes.w: The curved velocity-time graph shows the object slowing down as it falls.
mistakes.r: It is still speeding up but with decreasing acceleration until it reaches terminal velocity.

mistakes.w: Reading the time axis scale wrongly (e.g. each square = 1 s when it is 2 s).
mistakes.r: Check the value of one small square on each axis before reading or calculating.

exam.q: State what the gradient of a distance-time graph represents.
model: speed
exam.tip: One word answer; 'velocity' is accepted only if direction is implied.

exam.q: State what the area under a velocity-time graph represents.
model: distance travelled
exam.tip: Do not write 'displacement' unless asked; 'distance' is what the mark scheme rewards.

exam.q: Describe the motion shown by a horizontal line on (a) a distance-time graph and (b) a velocity-time graph.
model: (a) stationary / not moving
(b) constant velocity / constant speed / zero acceleration
exam.tip: The same shape means different things on different graphs.

exam.q: A distance-time graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (25 s, 200 m). Calculate the speed.
model: speed = 200 ÷ 25
= 8 m/s
exam.tip: Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time.

exam.q: A velocity-time graph shows a car going from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Calculate the acceleration and the distance travelled in this time.
model: a = 2 m/s²
distance = area = (4 × 6) + ½ × 6 × 12 (or ½ × (4 + 16) × 6)
exam.tip: Split the trapezium into a rectangle and a triangle if you are unsure.

exam.q: Explain why, without air resistance, a heavy ball and a light ball dropped together hit the ground at the same time.
model: heavier ball has larger weight but also larger mass
acceleration = force ÷ mass is the same (g = 10 m/s²) for both
exam.tip: Mention both force and mass, then link to equal acceleration.

exam.q: State the acceleration of an object in free fall near the Earth's surface.
model: about 10 m/s² (9.8 m/s²)
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: Higher: explain how to find the speed of an accelerating object at a time of 4 s from its curved distance-time graph.
model: draw a tangent to the curve at t = 4 s
draw a large triangle on the tangent and read Δd and Δt
speed = Δd ÷ Δt (gradient of tangent)
exam.tip: The word 'tangent' is the key mark.

exam.q: Higher: a velocity-time graph for a falling skydiver is curved. Each grid square is 5 m/s by 1 s and about 46 squares lie under the curve in the first 10 s. Estimate the distance fallen.
model: one square = 5 × 1 = 5 m
distance = 46 × 5 = 230 m
exam.tip: Work out the value of one square first.

exam.q: Describe and explain the shape of the velocity-time graph for a skydiver from leaving the plane until reaching terminal velocity.
model: at first only weight acts / drag is zero, so acceleration is 10 m/s² and the graph starts with gradient 10 m/s²
as speed increases, air resistance increases
resultant force (weight − drag) decreases
so acceleration decreases and the gradient of the graph decreases (curve gets less steep)
eventually drag = weight, resultant force zero
acceleration zero, graph horizontal: terminal velocity (constant velocity)
exam.tip: Link each change in the graph's gradient to a change in resultant force.

exam.q: A cyclist travels 300 m in 60 s, stops for 30 s, then travels 300 m in 50 s. Calculate her average speed for the whole journey.
model: total distance 600 m, total time 140 s
average speed = 600 ÷ 140 = 4.3 m/s
exam.tip: Include the stopped time in the total time.

worked.q: Use the velocity-time graph (0 to 10 m/s in 4 s, constant 10 m/s until 11 s, then to rest at 15 s) to find the total distance travelled and the average speed.
steps: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 110 ÷ 15 = 7.3 m/s.

worked.q: A tangent drawn to a curved distance-time graph passes through (2.0 s, 3.0 m) and (6.0 s, 23.0 m). Find the instantaneous speed at that point.
A stone falls from rest for 2.0 s with negligible air resistance. Use a velocity-time graph to find its speed after 2.0 s and the distance it has fallen (g = 10 m/s²).
steps: The graph is a straight line from 0 with gradient 10 m/s².
Distance = area of triangle = ½ × 2.0 × 20 = 20 m.

phy_ocrb.3.5.summary: Forces are vectors, so to find their combined effect you must take direction into account. The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together: forces in a line are added with signs, and forces at angles are added tip to tail on a scale vector diagram. Free body diagrams show every force acting on one object, and Higher candidates must resolve forces into components and recognise equilibrium as a closed vector diagram with zero resultant.

core.p: A force is a push or a pull caused by an interaction between objects. Force is a **vector**: it has a size (magnitude, in newtons, N) and a direction. That is why forces are drawn as arrows, and why you cannot simply add up the numbers when forces point in different directions.
bullets: Arrow length represents the **size** of the force (drawn to scale where possible).
Arrow direction shows the **direction** the force acts.
Arrow starts on the object the force acts on.
Unit: newton (N).
Examples: weight, normal contact force, friction, air resistance (drag), tension, thrust, upthrust.

core.p: When several forces act on one object, their combined effect is the same as one single force: the **resultant force**. It is the resultant force, not any single force, that decides how the object's motion changes.
bullets: Resultant force = the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together.
Also called the **net force**.
If the resultant force is zero, the forces are **balanced**.
If the resultant force is not zero, the forces are **unbalanced** and the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant.
The resultant can be found by calculation (forces in a line) or by a scale vector diagram (forces at angles).

callouts.p: The resultant force is the single force that would have the same effect on an object as all the original forces acting together.

core.h: Adding forces in a straight line
core.p: If all forces act along the same line, choose one direction as positive. Forces in that direction are positive, forces the opposite way are negative, and the resultant is the sum.
bullets: Same direction: **add** the sizes (30 N + 20 N to the right = 50 N to the right).
Opposite directions: **subtract** the smaller from the larger; the resultant points the way of the larger force.
Always give the direction as well as the size, for example '30 N to the right' or '200 N upwards'.
Consider horizontal and vertical forces separately if both act.
Example: a rocket with thrust 25 000 N upwards and weight 20 000 N has a resultant of 5000 N upwards.

callouts.p: A resultant force answer with no direction usually loses a mark. It is a vector.

core.h: Balanced and unbalanced forces and motion
core.p: The resultant force links forces to motion. This idea underpins Newton's first and second laws (covered in their own point), so you must be able to use it with free body diagrams.
bullets: Resultant force zero: a stationary object stays still; a moving object keeps moving at **constant speed in a straight line**.
Resultant force forwards: the object speeds up.
Resultant force backwards (against the motion): the object slows down.
Resultant force at an angle to the motion: the object changes direction.
Constant speed does NOT need a forward resultant force: it needs a zero resultant force.

core.p: A **free body diagram** shows one object on its own with ALL the forces acting **on** it, and no forces it exerts on other things. It is the standard way to show forces in OCR answers.
bullets: Draw the object as a simple box or dot.
Draw every force acting on the object as an arrow starting on the object.
Make arrow lengths proportional to force sizes (equal forces, equal lengths).
Label every arrow with its name and, if known, its size: weight, normal contact force, friction, drag, thrust, tension.
Do NOT include forces the object exerts on something else (the other force of each interaction pair acts on a different object).
Use the diagram to find the resultant force, horizontally and vertically.

callouts.p: Weight acts downwards from the centre of mass; the normal contact force acts upwards, at right angles to the surface.

core.h: Free body diagrams for common situations
core.p: OCR often asks you to complete or interpret a free body diagram for a familiar situation. Learn the forces involved in each.
bullets: **Object on a table**: weight down, normal contact force up, equal.
**Car at constant speed**: driving force forwards; air resistance and friction backwards (equal total); weight and normal contact force equal.
**Falling object**: weight down; air resistance up (grows with speed).
**Object hanging on a string**: weight down; tension up.
**Boat floating**: weight down; upthrust up.
**Object on a slope**: weight vertically down; normal contact force at right angles to the slope; friction along the slope opposing motion.

core.h: Scale vector diagrams: the tip-to-tail method
core.p: When forces act at angles, draw them to scale **tip to tail**. The resultant is the arrow that closes the gap from the start of the first force to the tip of the last one. Measuring that arrow gives the size and direction of the resultant.
bullets: Choose a sensible **scale** (for example 1 cm = 10 N) and write it down.
Draw the first force to scale in the correct direction using a ruler and protractor.
Draw the next force starting from the **tip** of the first one.
Draw the resultant from the **tail of the first** to the **tip of the last** force.
Measure its length and convert using the scale; measure its angle with a protractor.
Give the answer as size and direction, for example '50 N at 37° to the horizontal'.

callouts.p: A larger drawing gives a more accurate measurement. Use a sharp pencil and state your scale.

core.p: For two perpendicular forces the vector diagram is a right-angled triangle, so you can check a scale drawing with Pythagoras and trigonometry.
bullets: Resultant size = square root of (F1² + F2²).
Angle from F1: tan θ = F2 ÷ F1.
Example: 40 N east and 30 N north give a resultant of 50 N at 37° north of east.
The resultant of two forces is always smaller than their simple sum (70 N here) unless they point the same way.
OCR may ask for a scale drawing specifically: then you must draw, not just calculate.

core.p: The same tip-to-tail method works for any angle. You can also use the **parallelogram method**: draw both forces from the same point, complete the parallelogram, and the diagonal from the starting point is the resultant.
bullets: Two forces at a small angle give a resultant close to their sum.
Two forces at a wide angle (nearly opposite) give a small resultant.
Example: two 10 N forces at 120° to each other give a resultant of 10 N along the line halfway between them.
Example: a boat pulled by two ropes at angles moves along the line of the resultant force.
More than two forces: keep adding tip to tail; the order does not change the resultant.

core.h: Higher: resolving a force into components
core.p: Resolving is the reverse of adding: you replace one force with two forces at right angles (usually horizontal and vertical) that together have the same effect. This lets you see how much of a force acts in each direction.
bullets: Draw the force to scale as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
Draw the horizontal and vertical sides; measure them to find the components.
By trigonometry: horizontal component = F cos θ, vertical component = F sin θ (θ measured from the horizontal).
Example: a 100 N pull at 30° to the horizontal: horizontal 87 N, vertical 50 N.
On a slope, weight can be resolved into a component down the slope and a component into the slope.
Only the component in the direction of motion speeds an object up along that direction.

fig.cap: Higher tier: resolving a 100 N pull at 30° above the horizontal into two perpendicular components. Drawn to scale, the horizontal component is about 87 N and the vertical component is 50 N. Together the two components have exactly the same effect as the single force.

core.h: Higher: equilibrium and closed vector triangles
core.p: An object is in **equilibrium** when the resultant force on it is zero. If you draw all the forces tip to tail to scale, they form a **closed shape** (a triangle for three forces): the end of the last arrow meets the start of the first, so there is no resultant left over.
bullets: Equilibrium means the forces are balanced: the object is stationary or moving at constant velocity.
Three forces in equilibrium make a closed triangle when drawn tip to tail.
If the shape does not close, the gap is the resultant force.
Use this to find an unknown force: draw the known forces, and the arrow needed to close the triangle is the unknown force.
Example: a picture hanging from two strings; the two tensions and the weight form a closed triangle.
Equivalent test: the components of all the forces add to zero both horizontally and vertically.

callouts.p: Resultant force zero: vector diagram closes. Unbalanced: the gap needed to close it is the resultant.

core.h: Exam technique for force diagram questions
core.p: Force diagram questions reward precise drawing and full answers.
bullets: Use a ruler for every arrow and put arrowheads on.
Label forces with their proper names, not 'gravity force' or 'push from floor'.
State scale, measured length and converted value.
Give resultants with size AND direction.
Check by calculation (Pythagoras) where the forces are at right angles.
When asked to explain motion, link the resultant force to the change in motion.

analogy.t: Tug of war with extra teams
analogy.p: Picture a tug of war where several teams pull ropes tied to one ring. Each team is a force arrow: how hard they pull is the length, where they pull is the direction. The way the ring actually moves is the resultant force. If the teams are matched, the ring stays put (equilibrium) even though everyone is pulling hard. Where it breaks down: ropes can only pull, whereas real forces can also push, and the ring in a tug of war is usually stationary, while balanced forces can also mean steady motion at constant velocity.

terms.d: A push or pull on an object arising from an interaction with another object; a vector measured in newtons (N).
A quantity with magnitude and direction, such as force, velocity and acceleration.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, speed and energy.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together.
Another name for the resultant force.
Forces whose resultant is zero; the motion of the object does not change.
Forces with a non-zero resultant; the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant.
A diagram of one isolated object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows.
The force from a surface on an object, acting at right angles to the surface.
The gravitational force on an object, acting towards the centre of the Earth from the object's centre of mass.
A contact force that opposes sliding or the tendency to slide between surfaces.
The pulling force in a stretched rope, string or cable.
A diagram in which vectors are drawn to scale, tip to tail, to find the resultant by measurement.
Drawing each vector starting at the tip of the previous one; the resultant joins the first tail to the last tip.
Replacing a force with two perpendicular components that together have the same effect.
The part of a force acting in a particular direction, such as horizontal or vertical.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero; its vector diagram forms a closed shape.

mistakes.w: The car is moving at constant speed so the driving force is bigger than the friction.
mistakes.r: At constant speed the resultant force is zero: driving force equals the total resistive forces.

mistakes.w: Resultant force = 30 N (no direction).
mistakes.r: Give size and direction: 30 N to the right.

mistakes.w: Adding 40 N and 30 N at right angles to get 70 N.
mistakes.r: Use a scale diagram or Pythagoras: square root of (40² + 30²) = 50 N.

mistakes.w: Including the force the object exerts on the floor in its free body diagram.
mistakes.r: Only forces acting ON the object are drawn.

mistakes.w: Labelling forces 'gravity' and 'the ground pushing'.
mistakes.r: Use names that score: weight and normal contact force (reaction).

mistakes.w: Drawing arrows of random lengths on a free body diagram.
mistakes.r: Arrow lengths should be proportional to force sizes; balanced forces have equal-length arrows.

mistakes.w: Drawing the resultant from the tip of the first arrow.
mistakes.r: The resultant goes from the tail (start) of the first arrow to the tip of the last arrow.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to state the scale on a scale drawing.
mistakes.r: Write the scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 N) and show measured length and conversion.

mistakes.w: Equilibrium means the object is not moving.
mistakes.r: Equilibrium means resultant force is zero: the object is stationary OR moving at constant velocity.

exam.q: State what is meant by the resultant force on an object.
model: the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on the object combined
exam.tip: Key words: single force, same effect.

exam.q: A box has forces of 12 N to the left and 30 N to the right acting on it. Calculate the resultant force.
model: to the right
exam.tip: The direction mark is often separate.

exam.q: Draw a free body diagram for a book resting on a table.
model: weight arrow downwards and normal contact force arrow upwards, both labelled
arrows of equal length
exam.tip: Equal lengths show balanced forces.

exam.q: A lorry travels at a constant speed along a straight road. The driving force is 4500 N. State the total resistive force and explain your answer.
model: constant speed so resultant force is zero / forces balanced
exam.tip: Link constant velocity to zero resultant force.

exam.q: A rocket of weight 30 000 N produces 45 000 N of thrust at launch. Calculate the resultant force and describe the rocket's motion.
model: upwards
rocket accelerates upwards
exam.tip: Size, direction, then consequence.

exam.q: Two tugs pull a ship. One pulls with 3000 N due north, the other with 4000 N due east. Using a scale drawing, find the size and direction of the resultant force.
model: suitable scale stated, e.g. 1 cm = 500 N
vectors drawn tip to tail at right angles
resultant 5000 N (±100 N)
at about 37° north of east (or 53° east of north)
exam.tip: Marks for the drawing as well as the answer: show the scale and arrows.

exam.q: Explain why the resultant of a 6 N force and an 8 N force can be anything from 2 N to 14 N.
model: forces are vectors so the resultant depends on the angle between them
14 N when in the same direction, 2 N when opposite
exam.tip: Mention direction and the two extreme cases.

exam.q: Higher: a force of 200 N acts at 60° above the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal and vertical components.
model: horizontal = 200 cos 60° = 100 N
vertical = 200 sin 60° = 173 N (170 N)
exam.tip: cos for the component next to the angle, sin for the one opposite.

exam.q: Higher: three forces act on a hanging sign. When drawn tip to tail to scale, they form a closed triangle. State what this tells you about the sign.
model: the resultant force is zero
the sign is in equilibrium (stationary / no acceleration)
exam.tip: Closed shape means no resultant.

exam.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Using free body diagrams, describe and explain how the forces on the skydiver change from leaving the plane until reaching terminal velocity.
model: at first only weight acts (air resistance zero): large downward resultant
skydiver accelerates downwards, speed increases
air resistance increases as speed increases
resultant force (weight − air resistance) decreases, so acceleration decreases
eventually air resistance equals weight
resultant force zero, constant velocity (terminal velocity); free body diagram arrows equal length
exam.tip: Describe the arrows at each stage: weight stays the same length, air resistance grows until equal.

worked.q: A parachutist of weight 800 N experiences an air resistance of 650 N. Find the resultant force and describe the motion.
steps: Take downwards as positive: weight +800 N, air resistance −650 N.
The resultant is not zero, so the parachutist is still accelerating downwards (speeding up), but with less acceleration than g.

worked.q: A boat is pulled by a 60 N force due east and an 80 N force due north. Use a scale diagram (1 cm = 10 N) to find the resultant, and check by calculation.
steps: Draw 6.0 cm east, then from its tip 8.0 cm north.
Join the start to the final tip: it measures 10.0 cm, so the resultant is 100 N.
Measure the angle from east: about 53°.
Check: square root of (60² + 80²) = square root of 10 000 = 100 N; tan θ = 80 ÷ 60 gives θ = 53°.

worked.q: Higher: a child pulls a sledge with a force of 50 N along a rope at 40° above the horizontal. Find the horizontal and vertical components of the pull.
steps: Or by scale drawing: draw 5.0 cm at 40° and measure the horizontal (3.8 cm) and vertical (3.2 cm) sides.

phy_ocrb.3.6.summary: Momentum is mass × velocity, a vector measured in kg m/s that tells you how hard a moving object is to stop. In a closed system the total momentum before a collision or explosion equals the total momentum after, so you can predict velocities after crashes, recoil and rocket motion. A resultant force changes momentum: change in momentum = resultant force × time. For a fixed change in momentum, a longer time means a smaller force, which is how crumple zones, seat belts, airbags and helmets protect people.

core.p: **Momentum** is a measure of how hard it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both how much mass the object has and how fast it is moving. A slow lorry and a fast bullet can both have large momentum.
bullets: momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) × velocity (m/s)
In symbols: **p = m × v**.
Unit: **kg m/s** (kilogram metres per second).
Momentum is a **vector**: it has the same direction as the velocity.
A stationary object has zero momentum.
Doubling the mass or doubling the velocity doubles the momentum.

callouts.p: momentum = mass × velocity, p = mv, in kg m/s.

core.p: Because momentum is a vector, objects moving in opposite directions have momentum of opposite sign. Choose one direction as positive at the start of every problem and stick to it.
bullets: Momentum to the right (+), to the left (−), or up (+), down (−).
Two equal masses moving towards each other at equal speeds have a total momentum of zero.
When adding momenta, add with signs: 10 000 + (−15 000) = −5000 kg m/s.
A negative answer means the motion is in the negative direction: state this in words.
A ball bouncing back off a wall reverses its momentum, so its change in momentum is bigger than if it just stopped.

fig.cap: Momentum is a vector, so directions need signs. Taking right as positive, total momentum before = (1000 × 10) + (1500 × −10) = −5000 kg m/s. After sticking together, 2500 kg must have −5000 kg m/s, so the wreck moves at 2 m/s to the left.

core.p: In any collision or explosion, provided no external forces act, the total momentum stays the same. This is the **principle of conservation of momentum**. It is one of the most powerful ideas in physics because it works even when you do not know the forces involved.
bullets: Total momentum before = total momentum after.
It applies to a **closed system**: no external forces (such as friction) act on the objects.
Momentum can be passed from one object to another, but the total does not change.
It applies to collisions (objects hitting), explosions (objects pushing apart) and objects joining.
Kinetic energy is often NOT conserved in collisions (some is transferred to the surroundings as heating and sound), but momentum is.

callouts.p: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.

core.p: To solve a collision problem, write the total momentum before and after and set them equal.
bullets: Write: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2 (with signs for direction).
If the objects **stick together**, they move with one common velocity: (m1 + m2) × v.
If one object is initially stationary, its momentum before is zero.
Rearrange to find the unknown velocity or mass.
Check the direction of the answer makes sense.

callouts.p: Sketch two boxes, 'before' and 'after', with masses, velocities and arrows. It stops sign mistakes.

core.p: In an explosion the objects start at rest, so the total momentum before is zero. Afterwards the momenta must still add to zero, so the pieces move apart with **equal and opposite momentum**.
bullets: Gun or cannon firing: the bullet goes forwards, the gun **recoils** backwards.
The more massive object moves more slowly: m1v1 = −m2v2.
Rocket and jet engines: gas is pushed backwards, so the rocket gains forward momentum.
Two people on ice skates pushing apart move off in opposite directions; the lighter person moves faster.
Firing a hose or a balloon releasing air are everyday examples.

fig.cap: An explosion: a cannon fires a ball. Before firing, total momentum is zero. Afterwards the ball has +200 kg m/s (to the right) and the cannon recoils with −200 kg m/s (to the left), so the total is still zero. The heavy cannon moves much more slowly than the light ball.

core.p: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's third law. During a collision the two objects push on each other with **equal and opposite forces** for **the same time**. So one gains exactly as much momentum as the other loses.
bullets: Force of A on B = − force of B on A (interaction pair).
Both forces act for the same contact time t.
Change in momentum = force × time, so the changes are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Total change in momentum = 0, so total momentum is constant.
An external force (like friction from the ground) would change the total, which is why the system must be closed.

core.p: A resultant force acting on an object changes its momentum. The bigger the force and the longer it acts, the bigger the change.
bullets: change in momentum (kg m/s) = resultant force (N) × time for which it acts (s)
In symbols: **Δp = F × t**, so F = Δp ÷ t.
Δp = mv − mu (final momentum minus initial momentum).
Units check: N s is the same as kg m/s.
This is Newton's second law in another form: F = (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t = ma.
The force is equal to the **rate of change of momentum**.

callouts.p: The same change in momentum can come from a large force for a short time or a small force for a long time.

core.p: In a crash, the change in momentum is fixed by the mass and the speed: the car (and the person) must go from moving to stopped. Since F = Δp ÷ t, making the stopping **time longer** makes the **force smaller**, which reduces injuries.
bullets: **Crumple zones** at the front and back of a car crush in a collision, increasing the time for the car to stop.
**Seat belts** stretch slightly, so the passenger slows down over a longer time and does not hit the dashboard.
**Airbags** inflate and squash slowly, increasing the time for the head to stop and spreading the force over a larger area.
**Cycle and motorcycle helmets** have crushable foam linings that increase the stopping time of the head.
**Crash mats, soft playground surfaces and sand pits** increase landing time.
**Bending your knees** when landing from a jump increases the stopping time.

head: Safety feature
How it changes the time
Effect on force
rows: crushes, car stops over longer time
squashes, head stops over longer time

callouts.p: Do not write that safety features 'absorb the impact'. Say they INCREASE THE TIME of the collision, so the rate of change of momentum, and therefore the force, is SMALLER.

core.p: The same equation explains sports techniques. Sometimes you want a big change in momentum (hitting a ball hard), sometimes a small force (catching).
bullets: **Catching**: pulling your hands back increases the stopping time, so the force on your hands is smaller.
**Follow-through** in tennis, golf or cricket keeps the racket or club in contact with the ball for longer, so for the same force the ball gains a larger change in momentum and leaves faster.
Goalkeepers' gloves and boxing gloves are padded to increase impact time.
Rugby tackles: a heavier, faster player has more momentum and is harder to stop.

core.h: Calculating force from a change in momentum
core.p: OCR often combines the momentum equation with Δp = F × t. Work step by step.
bullets: 1. Find the initial momentum (mu) and final momentum (mv), with signs.
2. Change in momentum = mv − mu.
3. Force = change in momentum ÷ time (convert ms to s: 1 ms = 0.001 s).
4. Give the unit (N) and direction if needed.
If the object bounces back, the change in momentum is m(v + u) in size, because the velocity reverses.

core.p: You may be asked to estimate the size of a force in an everyday collision using sensible values.
bullets: Car occupant: mass about 70 kg, speed about 15 m/s.
Without a seat belt, stopping time on hitting the dashboard might be about 0.01 s: F = (70 × 15) ÷ 0.01 = 105 000 N.
With a seat belt and airbag, stopping time might be about 0.2 s: F = 1050 ÷ 0.2 = 5250 N, twenty times smaller.
Estimates should be given to 1 or 2 significant figures.
This is why stopping a vehicle suddenly is so dangerous: huge forces from very short times.

core.p: Momentum questions reward clear layout and correct use of directions.
bullets: Always state which direction you have taken as positive.
Show 'momentum before' and 'momentum after' as separate lines.
For explanation questions use the chain: same change in momentum, longer time, smaller rate of change of momentum, smaller force.
Remember the unit kg m/s (or N s) for momentum, N for force.
Check whether objects stick together or move separately after the collision.

analogy.t: Momentum as money passed between friends
analogy.p: Think of momentum as money and a collision as two friends swapping cash. However they swap, the total amount of money between them stays the same, just as total momentum is conserved. An outside force is like a bank paying in or taking out money, which changes the total, so the rule only works for a closed system. Where it breaks down: money cannot be negative in your pocket, but momentum can be negative because it has a direction, so two friends can 'have' +5 and −5 and a total of zero while both are moving.

terms.d: Mass multiplied by velocity (p = mv); a vector measured in kg m/s.
The unit of momentum; equivalent to the newton second (N s).
A quantity with size and direction; momentum takes the direction of the velocity.
In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after.
A group of objects on which no external resultant force acts.
An event in which objects hit and exert forces on each other for a short time.
An event in which objects initially at rest together are pushed apart; total momentum stays zero.
The backward movement of a gun or cannon when it fires, due to conservation of momentum.
Final momentum minus initial momentum; equal to resultant force × time for which it acts.
Change in momentum divided by time; equal to the resultant force.
Force × time; equal to the change in momentum it produces.
Part of a car designed to crush in a collision, increasing stopping time and so reducing force.
A strap that stretches slightly to slow a passenger over a longer time, reducing the force.
A bag that inflates in a crash, increasing the time for the occupant to stop and spreading the force.
When two objects interact they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.

mistakes.w: Momentum unit given as kg/m s or N.
mistakes.r: kg m/s (or N s).

mistakes.w: Ignoring direction: adding momenta of objects moving in opposite directions.
mistakes.r: Choose a positive direction and give opposite momenta a minus sign.

mistakes.w: The airbag absorbs the force.
mistakes.r: The airbag increases the time taken to stop, so the rate of change of momentum and the force are reduced.

mistakes.w: The crumple zone reduces the change in momentum.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same; the time is longer so the force is smaller.

mistakes.w: Using only the mass of the moving trolley after they stick together.
mistakes.r: Use the combined mass (m1 + m2) after objects join.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved so kinetic energy is too.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved in all collisions; kinetic energy usually is not.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert milliseconds to seconds.
mistakes.r: Divide ms by 1000 before using F = Δp ÷ t.

mistakes.w: Total momentum before an explosion is the momentum of the bullet.
mistakes.r: Before an explosion everything is at rest, so the total momentum is zero.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved even when friction acts strongly.
mistakes.r: Conservation applies only when no external forces act (a closed system).

exam.q: State the equation linking momentum, mass and velocity.
model: momentum = mass × velocity
exam.tip: Recall equation: must be learnt.

exam.q: Calculate the momentum of a 1200 kg car moving at 25 m/s.
exam.tip: Unit kg m/s.

exam.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
model: in a closed system / with no external forces, total momentum before = total momentum after
exam.tip: Mention 'total' and 'before and after'.

exam.q: A 3.0 kg trolley moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
model: momentum before = 3.0 × 4.0 = 12 kg m/s
exam.tip: Combined mass after sticking.

exam.q: A rifle of mass 4.0 kg fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
model: total momentum before = 0
0.010 × 400 = 4.0 kg m/s so rifle momentum = −4.0 kg m/s
v = −4.0 ÷ 4.0 = 1.0 m/s backwards
exam.tip: State the direction: opposite to the bullet.

exam.q: A footballer kicks a 0.45 kg ball from rest to 20 m/s. The foot is in contact for 0.009 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
model: change in momentum = 0.45 × 20 = 9.0 kg m/s
exam.tip: Force = change in momentum ÷ time.

exam.q: State the equation that links change in momentum, resultant force and time.
model: change in momentum = resultant force × time for which it acts
exam.tip: Say 'resultant' force for full credit.

exam.q: Explain how a cycle helmet reduces the risk of head injury in a fall.
model: foam lining crushes / compresses
increases the time taken for the head to stop
same change in momentum, so smaller force on the head (F = Δp ÷ t)
exam.tip: Key chain: longer time, same change in momentum, smaller force.

exam.q: Explain why a cricketer moves their hands backwards when catching a fast ball.
model: increases the time taken to stop the ball
so the force on the hands is reduced (smaller rate of change of momentum)
exam.tip: Do not say 'absorbs the momentum'.

exam.q: Describe how car safety features use ideas about momentum to reduce injuries in a crash. Refer to at least two features.
model: in a crash the occupant's momentum changes from mv to zero; this change in momentum is fixed
force = change in momentum ÷ time, so a longer stopping time gives a smaller force
crumple zones crush, increasing the time for the car to stop
seat belts stretch, increasing the time for the passenger to stop and preventing hitting the windscreen
airbags inflate and squash, increasing the stopping time of the head and spreading force over a larger area
smaller forces mean less serious injuries
exam.tip: Level 3 needs the physics explanation (force = Δp ÷ t) linked to each feature, not just a list of features.

exam.q: Higher: show that the equation F = (mv − mu) ÷ t is equivalent to F = ma.
model: (mv − mu) ÷ t = m(v − u) ÷ t
(v − u) ÷ t = a, so F = ma
exam.tip: Factorise m, then use the definition of acceleration.

worked.q: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 8.0 m/s hits a wall and stops in 0.040 s. Calculate the change in momentum and the average force on the ball.
steps: Initial momentum = 0.50 × 8.0 = 4.0 kg m/s; final momentum = 0.
Change in momentum = 0 − 4.0 = −4.0 kg m/s (size 4.0 kg m/s).
Force = change in momentum ÷ time = 4.0 ÷ 0.040 = 100 N.
The force on the ball is 100 N, directed away from the wall (opposite to its original motion).
worked.ans: Change in momentum 4.0 kg m/s; average force 100 N

worked.q: A 1000 kg car at 10 m/s to the right collides head-on with a 1500 kg car at 10 m/s to the left. They stick together. Find their velocity just after the collision.
steps: After: total mass 2500 kg, momentum still −5000 kg m/s (conservation of momentum).

worked.q: A 60 kg skater at rest pushes off a 40 kg skater, also at rest. The 60 kg skater moves away at 2.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the 40 kg skater.
steps: The minus sign means opposite direction to the 60 kg skater.

phy_ocrb.3.7.summary: Newton's first law says an object keeps its velocity (stays at rest or moves at constant speed in a straight line) unless a non-zero resultant force acts. Newton's second law says the resultant force causes an acceleration in its own direction, with resultant force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). Inertial mass measures how hard it is to change an object's velocity (m = F ÷ a), and an object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating because its direction changes, so it needs a resultant force towards the centre.

core.p: A force is needed to **change** the way something moves, not to keep it moving. What matters is the **resultant force**: the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together. Newton's first and second laws tell you what happens when the resultant force is zero and when it is not.
bullets: Resultant force = vector sum of all forces acting **on one object**.
Forces in the same line: add if same direction, subtract if opposite.
Zero resultant force: the forces are **balanced**.
Non-zero resultant force: the object **accelerates** in the direction of the resultant force.
Acceleration can mean speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

callouts.p: Motion does not need a force. A **change in motion** (a change in velocity) needs a resultant force.

core.p: Newton's first law says that if the resultant force on an object is zero, its velocity does not change. A stationary object stays still, and a moving object carries on at the **same speed in the same direction**.
bullets: Zero resultant force + object at rest: it **remains at rest**.
Zero resultant force + moving object: it continues at **constant speed in a straight line** (constant velocity).
So a car cruising at a steady 30 m/s on a straight road has **driving force = resistive forces**.
A skydiver at **terminal velocity** has weight = air resistance, so the resultant force is zero.
On Earth things seem to stop on their own only because **friction and air resistance** provide a resultant force backwards.
In deep space, with no resistive forces, a spacecraft keeps moving without its engines.

callouts.p: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object remains at rest or continues to move in a straight line at a constant speed.
A moving object does not need a forward resultant force to keep moving. Constant velocity means **balanced** forces.

core.h: Newton's second law and F = ma
core.p: When the resultant force is not zero, the object accelerates. The acceleration is **proportional to the resultant force** and **inversely proportional to the mass**. This is summed up in the equation F = m × a.
bullets: **Resultant force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²)**, F = m × a.
Rearranged: a = F ÷ m and m = F ÷ a.
1 newton is the resultant force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Double the resultant force on the same mass: acceleration **doubles**.
Double the mass with the same resultant force: acceleration **halves**.
The acceleration is always in the **same direction as the resultant force**.
Always use the **resultant** force in F = ma, never just one of the forces.

callouts.p: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass: resultant force = mass × acceleration.
F = m × a must be recalled, not just found on the equation sheet.

core.h: Using free body diagrams with F = ma
core.p: Most F = ma questions first ask you to find the resultant force. Draw the object, add every force as an arrow from the object, then combine the forces in each direction.
bullets: Step 1: list all forces acting **on** the object (weight, normal contact force, driving force, friction, drag, tension).
Step 2: find the resultant in the direction of motion (forward forces − backward forces).
Step 3: use a = F ÷ m and state the **direction** of the acceleration.
If the resultant is backwards, the object **decelerates** (negative acceleration).
Vertical forces on a car on a level road balance, so they do not affect horizontal acceleration.

core.p: Inertia is the tendency of an object to **keep doing what it is already doing**, staying still or moving at constant velocity. The more mass an object has, the harder it is to change its velocity. Higher tier students must define inertial mass.
bullets: **Inertia**: the tendency of an object to remain at rest or in uniform motion.
**Inertial mass** measures how difficult it is to change an object's velocity.
Inertial mass = resultant force ÷ acceleration, m = F ÷ a.
A loaded lorry is hard to start and hard to stop because of its large inertial mass.
A shopping trolley full of bottles needs a much bigger push for the same acceleration than an empty one.
Inertial mass is the same quantity as the mass in kg you weigh on scales; it does not change with location (unlike weight).

callouts.p: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. It is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration, m = F ÷ a.

core.h: Why bigger mass means smaller acceleration
core.p: The same push on a larger mass produces less acceleration, because the push has more matter to speed up. The graph shows that acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force, and the gradient is 1 ÷ mass.
bullets: For a fixed mass: a ∝ F, so a graph of a against F is a **straight line through the origin**.
Gradient of the a against F graph = 1 ÷ m, so a **steeper line means smaller mass**.
For a fixed force: a ∝ 1/m, so doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
This is why lorries accelerate slowly from traffic lights compared with motorbikes.
You may investigate this with a trolley pulled by hanging masses on a runway (PAG3, covered with acceleration).

core.h: Applying Newton's laws to everyday motion
core.p: Exam questions often describe a journey and ask you to link each stage to the forces. Decide whether the velocity is changing and then whether the resultant force is zero.
bullets: Car pulling away: driving force > resistive forces, so resultant forwards, accelerates.
Car at steady speed: driving force = resistive forces, resultant zero (first law).
Car braking: braking force + resistive forces backwards, resultant backwards, decelerates.
Skydiver just after jumping: weight > air resistance, accelerates downwards.
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force and acceleration **decrease**.
At terminal velocity: weight = air resistance, constant velocity.
Parachute opens: air resistance > weight, resultant upwards, decelerates to a new lower terminal velocity.

core.p: An object moving in a circle at **constant speed** is still **accelerating**, because its direction, and so its velocity, is continually changing. Velocity is a vector, so a change in direction is a change in velocity.
bullets: Speed is a scalar (size only); velocity is a vector (size and direction).
In a circle the **direction** of motion changes all the time, so velocity changes.
A changing velocity is an **acceleration**, even if the speed stays the same.
The velocity at any moment is along the **tangent** to the circle.
If the force stopped, the object would fly off along the tangent (Newton's first law).

callouts.p: Constant speed in a circle = changing velocity = acceleration = a resultant force is acting.

core.h: Circular motion: the force towards the centre
core.p: Because the object accelerates, Newton's second law says there must be a resultant force. For motion in a circle this resultant force acts **towards the centre of the circle**, at right angles to the velocity.
bullets: The resultant force is directed **towards the centre** (centripetal force).
It acts at **90° to the velocity**, so it changes direction but not speed.
No work is done by this force on the object, so its kinetic energy and speed stay constant.
Examples: **gravity** keeps the Moon and satellites in orbit around the Earth.
**Tension** in the string keeps a ball whirled on a string moving in a circle.
**Friction** between tyres and road lets a car go round a bend.
A faster speed, a larger mass or a tighter circle all need a **bigger** force towards the centre.

callouts.p: There is no outward 'centrifugal' force on the object. The resultant force is inwards; you feel thrown outwards because your body tends to carry on in a straight line.

core.p: Any force with a component at right angles to the motion changes the direction of travel. This links circular motion to other examples of forces causing a change in direction.
bullets: A force **along** the motion changes speed only.
A force **at right angles** to the motion changes direction only.
A force at another angle changes both speed and direction.
Projectile: gravity acts down while the object moves sideways, so the path curves.
A satellite orbits because gravity pulls it towards Earth at 90° to its velocity.

core.p: Calculation questions are worth easy marks if you set them out clearly. Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit and sensible significant figures.
bullets: Convert grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) and kN to N (× 1000) first.
Find acceleration from a = (v − u) ÷ t if you are given speeds and a time.
Then F = m × a gives the resultant force needed.
If a question asks for the driving force, add the resistive forces to the resultant force.
Negative acceleration means the resultant force is opposite to the motion.

callouts.p: Write the equation in words or symbols before substituting. If you make an arithmetic slip you can still earn the method mark.

analogy.p: Imagine pushing supermarket trolleys. An empty trolley rolling across a smooth floor keeps going until something stops it (first law). Push harder and it speeds up faster; fill it with bottles and the same push speeds it up much less (second law: more inertial mass, less acceleration). Swinging it round a corner, you must pull it sideways towards the centre of the turn, not push it outwards. Where it breaks down: a real trolley slows down because of friction, which can make it seem that motion needs a force; in the physics model with no friction it would roll on forever. Also your push is just one force, while F = ma uses the resultant of all forces.

If the resultant force on an object is zero, it stays at rest or moves at constant speed in a straight line.
Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass: F = m × a.
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Rate of change of velocity, in m/s²; a vector in the direction of the resultant force.

Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity.
The tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving with the same velocity.

The resultant force on an object moving in a circle, directed towards the centre of the circle.
The direction of the velocity of an object in circular motion, at 90° to the radius.

mistakes.r: Constant velocity means the forces are balanced: driving force = resistive forces, resultant force zero.

mistakes.w: Using one force (e.g. the engine force) in F = ma.
mistakes.r: Use the resultant force: driving force minus resistive forces.

mistakes.w: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is not accelerating.
mistakes.r: Its direction changes, so its velocity changes, so it is accelerating.

mistakes.w: The force on an object in a circle acts outwards.
mistakes.r: The resultant force acts towards the centre of the circle.

mistakes.w: Mass and weight are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Mass (kg) measures inertia and does not change; weight (N) is the gravitational force and depends on g.

mistakes.w: No force means the object stops.
mistakes.r: With zero resultant force a moving object continues at constant velocity.

mistakes.r: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the object's velocity, defined as force ÷ acceleration.

exam.q: State Newton's first law of motion.
model: If the resultant force on an object is zero
it stays at rest or continues to move at constant speed in a straight line
exam.tip: Say 'resultant force is zero', not 'no forces act'.

exam.q: A resultant force of 600 N acts on a motorbike of mass 240 kg. Calculate its acceleration.
exam.tip: Rearrange F = ma before substituting.

exam.q: A car of mass 1500 kg accelerates at 2.0 m/s². The resistive forces are 800 N. Calculate the driving force.
model: Resultant force = m × a = 1500 × 2.0 = 3000 N
Driving force − resistive force = resultant force
Driving force = 3000 + 800 = 3800 N
exam.tip: F = ma gives the resultant, not the driving force.

exam.q: Explain why a cyclist riding at a steady speed on a straight level road must keep pedalling.
model: Friction and air resistance act backwards on the cyclist
Pedalling provides a forward force equal to these, so resultant is zero and velocity stays constant
exam.tip: Link to the first law: balanced forces, constant velocity.

exam.q: Explain why a satellite moving in a circular orbit at constant speed is accelerating.
model: Its direction of motion is constantly changing
Velocity is a vector, so its velocity is changing
A change in velocity is an acceleration (towards the centre, caused by gravity)
exam.tip: Use the words 'velocity' and 'direction' explicitly.

exam.q: State the direction of the resultant force on a ball whirled in a horizontal circle on a string, and name the force that provides it.
model: Towards the centre of the circle
Tension in the string
exam.tip: Never say 'outwards'.

exam.q: Define inertial mass. (Higher)
model: A measure of how difficult it is to change an object's velocity
The ratio of resultant force to acceleration (m = F ÷ a)
exam.tip: Learn both parts of the definition.

exam.q: A force of 45 N gives a block an acceleration of 1.5 m/s². Calculate the inertial mass of the block.
model: = 30 kg
exam.tip: Inertial mass has unit kg.

exam.q: A trolley is pulled by a constant resultant force. The mass of the trolley is doubled. Describe the effect on its acceleration and explain why.
model: The acceleration halves
Because a = F ÷ m / acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (greater inertial mass)
exam.tip: 'Halves' is better than 'decreases'.

exam.q: A car is travelling at 15 m/s. It accelerates uniformly to 25 m/s in 4.0 s. The mass of the car is 1200 kg. Calculate the resultant force on the car.
exam.tip: Two-step problems: find a first, then F.

exam.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Describe and explain the motion of the skydiver from leaving the plane until reaching terminal velocity, using Newton's laws.
model: At first the only significant force is weight, so the resultant force is downwards
The skydiver accelerates downwards (second law, a = F ÷ m)
As speed increases, air resistance increases
So the resultant force decreases and the acceleration decreases
Eventually air resistance equals weight, so the resultant force is zero
The skydiver moves at constant velocity, terminal velocity (first law)
exam.tip: 6-mark answers need a logical chain: force, resultant, acceleration, at each stage.

worked.q: A lorry of mass 12 000 kg has a driving force of 9000 N and resistive forces of 3000 N. Calculate its acceleration.
worked.ans: 0.50 m/s² in the direction of the driving force

worked.q: A trolley is pushed with a resultant force of 18 N and accelerates at 0.60 m/s². Calculate its inertial mass. Then calculate the acceleration if 10 kg of shopping is added and the force is unchanged.
worked.ans: Inertial mass 30 kg; new acceleration 0.45 m/s²

worked.q: A car of mass 1000 kg travelling at 20 m/s brakes to rest in 5.0 s. Calculate the resultant force on the car.
steps: The negative sign shows the force is opposite to the motion
worked.ans: 4000 N acting backwards (opposite to the direction of motion)

phy_ocrb.3.8.summary: The moment of a force is its turning effect about a pivot: moment (N m) = force (N) × perpendicular distance (m) from the pivot to the line of the force. When an object is balanced, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment (principle of moments). Levers and gears transmit the rotational effects of forces: a force applied far from a pivot, or a small gear driving a large gear, gives a larger moment at the cost of a larger movement or slower turning.

core.p: A force can make an object **turn** about a pivot as well as move it. The turning effect of a force is called its **moment**. The size of the moment depends on both the force and how far from the pivot it acts.
bullets: Moment of a force = force × distance, where the distance is measured **normal (perpendicular) to the direction of the force** from the pivot.
Moment is measured in **newton metres, N m**.
A bigger force gives a bigger moment.
The same force further from the pivot gives a bigger moment.
A force whose line of action passes **through the pivot** has zero moment.
Moments can be **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**.

callouts.p: Moment of a force (N m) = force (N) × distance (m) (normal to direction of the force).
You must recall this equation; it is not always given.

core.p: The distance in the moment equation is the shortest distance from the pivot to the **line of action** of the force. This is the distance at right angles to the force, not just any distance along the object.
bullets: Pushing at 90° to a door or spanner gives the **largest moment** for a given force.
Pushing at an angle reduces the perpendicular distance, so the moment is smaller.
Pushing straight towards the hinge gives zero perpendicular distance and **no turning effect**.
Always convert cm to m before calculating in N m (e.g. 25 cm = 0.25 m).

callouts.p: Using the distance along a slanted bar rather than the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force.

core.p: Many tools are designed to make the distance from the pivot large, so that a small force produces a large moment.
bullets: **Door handles** are placed far from the hinges.
**Long spanners** loosen tight nuts more easily.
**Wheelbarrows** have long handles so a small lift supports a heavy load.
**Bottle openers**, **crowbars** and **scissors** all use a pivot.
Cranes use a **counterweight** to balance the moment of the load.

core.p: If an object is **balanced** (in equilibrium and not turning), the turning effects in each direction cancel out.
bullets: For a balanced object: **total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment** about any pivot.
Add up all the clockwise moments, and separately all the anticlockwise moments.
If the clockwise total is larger, the object turns clockwise.
A small weight far from the pivot can balance a large weight close to the pivot.
A balanced object also has zero resultant force: the pivot pushes up with a force equal to the total weight.

callouts.p: When an object is balanced, the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same pivot.

core.p: Balance questions usually give you all but one force or distance. Write the principle of moments as an equation and rearrange.
bullets: Step 1: choose the pivot and identify each force and its perpendicular distance.
Step 2: decide whether each force turns the object clockwise or anticlockwise.
Step 3: write: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments.
Step 4: substitute, then solve for the unknown force or distance.
Step 5: give the unit (N, m or N m).

core.p: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a pivot. It **transmits the rotational effect of a force** from where you apply an effort to where it moves a load. Because the moments balance, a small effort a long way from the pivot can move a large load close to the pivot.
bullets: Effort × distance of effort from pivot = load × distance of load from pivot (when balanced).
Effort far from the pivot, load close: lever acts as a **force multiplier** (crowbar, wheelbarrow).
Effort close to the pivot, load far: the load moves further and faster but needs a bigger effort (e.g. your forearm, tweezers).
A lever does not give you energy for free: the effort moves a **larger distance** than the load.
Work done by effort = work done on load (if there is no friction).

head: Lever
Pivot position
Effect
rows: Small lift on handles supports heavy load
Hand moves far and fast; muscle force large

callouts.p: A rigid bar that turns about a pivot and transmits the rotational effect of a force.

core.p: Gears are wheels with teeth that **mesh** together. When one gear turns, its teeth push on the teeth of the next gear, so the rotational effect of a force is transmitted from one shaft to another.
bullets: The gear that is turned by the motor or pedal is the **driver** gear; the one it turns is the **driven** gear.
Two meshing gears turn in **opposite directions**.
At the point of contact the teeth push each other with **equal and opposite forces**.
Moment on each gear = this force × the radius of that gear.
So a **larger gear** experiences a **larger moment** from the same contact force.
The teeth must move at the same speed where they meet, so the larger gear turns **more slowly** (fewer turns per second).
A third gear placed between them (an idler) makes the output turn in the **same direction** as the input.

callouts.p: Small gear driving a large gear: the output turns more slowly but with a larger moment. Large gear driving a small gear: the output turns faster but with a smaller moment.

fig.cap: A 10-tooth driver gear turning clockwise meshes with a 20-tooth driven gear, which turns anticlockwise. The driven gear has twice the radius, so it turns at half the rate but the moment on it is doubled.

core.p: The number of teeth is proportional to the radius of the gear, so you can compare gears using the number of teeth.
bullets: Gear ratio = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear.
Moment on driven gear = moment on driver × gear ratio (ignoring friction).
Turns of driven gear = turns of driver ÷ gear ratio.
Example: 10 teeth driving 30 teeth, ratio 3: output turns 3 times slower with 3 times the moment.
Energy is conserved: a larger moment comes with a slower turning speed.

core.p: Choosing the right gear means trading turning speed for turning force.
bullets: **Bicycle** low gear: small front chainring and large rear sprocket give a large moment on the back wheel for going uphill or starting.
**Bicycle** high gear: large front and small rear give fast wheel rotation on flat roads.
**Car gearbox**: first gear gives a large moment to accelerate from rest; higher gears give high speed.
**Electric screwdrivers** and **drills** use gears to slow a fast motor and increase the moment.
**Clocks** use gear trains so the hands turn at different rates.

core.h: Linking moments to the rest of P4
core.p: Moments connect to forces and energy elsewhere in the chapter, and examiners like links between topics.
bullets: Balanced object: resultant force zero **and** resultant moment zero.
A lever or gear transfers energy by doing work; it cannot increase the energy transferred.
Friction in gears and pivots wastes some energy as heating, so real machines are less efficient.
Oil or grease reduces friction in gears.

callouts.p: When explaining a gear or lever, always mention force, distance from pivot (or radius) and moment, and say what happens to speed or distance moved.

analogy.p: Pushing a heavy door near its handle is easy; pushing right next to the hinges is almost impossible, even though you are the same person pushing just as hard. The hinge is the pivot, your push is the force, and the distance from the hinge multiplies its turning effect. Gears are like two people turning a revolving door from different radii: the person further out needs less force but has to walk further. Where it breaks down: the door is not balanced while it swings, so the principle of moments does not apply, and real hinges and gears waste some energy through friction.

terms.d: The turning effect of a force about a pivot; force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
The fixed point about which an object turns.
The unit of moment: a force of 1 N acting 1 m (perpendicular) from a pivot.
The shortest distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, at 90° to the force.
The line along which a force acts, extended in both directions.
A moment that tends to turn an object the same way as clock hands.
A moment that tends to turn an object the opposite way to clock hands.
For a balanced object, the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.
A state where the resultant force and the resultant moment on an object are both zero.
A rigid bar turning about a pivot that transmits the rotational effect of a force.
The force applied to a lever or machine.
The force that a lever or machine moves or overcomes.
A lever or gear system in which a small input force produces a larger output force.
A toothed wheel that meshes with another to transmit the rotational effect of a force.
The input gear, turned by the motor, pedal or handle.
The output gear, turned by the driver gear.
Number of teeth on the driven gear divided by the number of teeth on the driver gear.

mistakes.w: Moment = force ÷ distance.
mistakes.r: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.

mistakes.w: Using distance in cm and giving the answer in N m.
mistakes.r: Convert cm to m first (or give the unit N cm).

mistakes.w: Using the distance along the bar when the force is at an angle.
mistakes.r: Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

mistakes.w: A balanced object has equal forces on each side.
mistakes.r: A balanced object has equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments; the forces can be different.

mistakes.w: Meshing gears turn in the same direction.
mistakes.r: Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions.

mistakes.w: A larger driven gear turns faster.
mistakes.r: A larger driven gear turns more slowly but with a larger moment.

mistakes.w: Levers create extra energy.
mistakes.r: Levers multiply force but the effort moves further; energy is conserved (or some is wasted).

mistakes.w: Unit of moment written as N/m.
mistakes.r: The unit is N m (newton metre).

exam.q: State the equation that links moment of a force, force and distance.
model: Moment = force × distance (normal to the direction of the force)
exam.tip: Include 'perpendicular' or 'normal to the force' for full credit.

exam.q: A force of 40 N is applied at right angles to a spanner, 0.25 m from the nut. Calculate the moment.
model: Moment = 40 × 0.25
= 10 N m
exam.tip: Always give the unit N m.

exam.q: Explain why it is easier to open a door by pushing near the handle than near the hinge.
model: The handle is a larger (perpendicular) distance from the pivot/hinge
So a smaller force produces the same moment needed to open the door
exam.tip: Name the pivot and use the word 'moment'.

exam.q: State the principle of moments.
model: For a balanced object / in equilibrium
the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about a pivot
exam.tip: Say 'sum of' or 'total' moments.

exam.q: A child of weight 300 N sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Calculate where a child of weight 400 N must sit on the other side to balance it.
model: Anticlockwise moment = 300 × 2.0 = 600 N m
Clockwise moment = 400 × d = 600
exam.tip: Write the principle of moments as an equation first.

exam.q: A metre rule is pivoted at its centre. A 2.0 N weight hangs 30 cm to the left of the pivot and a 1.5 N weight hangs 20 cm to the right. Determine whether the rule balances.
model: Anticlockwise moment = 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.60 N m
Clockwise moment = 1.5 × 0.20 = 0.30 N m
Not balanced: the rule turns anticlockwise (left side goes down)
exam.tip: State the direction it turns, not just 'no'.

exam.q: Two gears mesh. The driver gear has 12 teeth and the driven gear has 36 teeth. Describe how the speed of rotation and the moment of the driven gear compare with the driver gear.
model: The driven gear turns 3 times more slowly / one third the rate
The moment on the driven gear is 3 times larger
exam.tip: Use the ratio of teeth (36 ÷ 12 = 3).

exam.q: State the direction of rotation of a driven gear when the driver gear turns clockwise.
model: Anticlockwise
exam.tip: Meshing gears always turn in opposite directions.

exam.q: A wheelbarrow carries a load of 600 N acting 0.40 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.2 m from the axle. Calculate the upward force needed on the handles to hold the wheelbarrow balanced.
model: Moment of load = 600 × 0.40 = 240 N m
Effort × 1.2 = 240
Effort = 200 N
exam.tip: The wheel axle is the pivot.

exam.q: A cyclist changes to a larger rear sprocket when going up a steep hill. Explain, in terms of forces and moments, why this helps. You should describe how levers and gears transmit the rotational effect of forces.
model: The cyclist's foot pushes on the pedal crank, which acts as a lever about the axle, producing a moment
The chainring pulls the chain with a force; the chain pulls on the rear sprocket
Moment on the rear sprocket = chain force × sprocket radius
A larger rear sprocket has a larger radius, so a larger moment acts on the back wheel
Larger moment on the wheel gives a larger forward force at the road to overcome the slope
But the wheel turns fewer times per pedal turn, so the bike moves more slowly for the same pedalling rate
exam.tip: Link each step: force, radius, moment, and say what is traded off.

worked.q: A uniform plank is pivoted at its centre. A 500 N weight is placed 1.2 m to the left of the pivot. Where must a 750 N weight be placed to balance it?
steps: For balance, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
worked.ans: 0.80 m to the right of the pivot

worked.q: A crowbar is used to lift a rock. The pivot is 0.10 m from the rock, which pushes down with 900 N. The worker pushes at 90° to the bar, 1.5 m from the pivot. Calculate the minimum force needed.
steps: Effort moment must equal 90 N m
worked.ans: 60 N, only one fifteenth of the load, because the effort is 15 times further from the pivot

worked.q: A motor turns a 15-tooth gear with a moment of 0.40 N m. It drives a 45-tooth gear. Ignoring friction, find the moment on the driven gear and how many turns it makes when the motor gear turns 90 times.
steps: Moment on driven gear = 0.40 × 3 = 1.2 N m

phy_ocrb.3.9.summary: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance is the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (typically 0.2 to 0.9 s), so it increases with speed, tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions; braking distance increases with speed, mass and poor road, tyre or brake conditions. Large decelerations need large forces that cause injury, so safety features such as crumple zones, seat belts, air bags and helmets increase the time taken to stop, reducing the rate of change of momentum and so the force.

core.p: When a driver sees a hazard, the car keeps moving while the driver reacts and then while the brakes slow it down. The total distance is the **stopping distance**.
bullets: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.**
**Thinking distance**: distance travelled during the driver's **reaction time**, at constant speed.
**Braking distance**: distance travelled while the **braking force** slows the vehicle to rest.
For a given braking force, the greater the speed, the greater the stopping distance.
Speed limits and safe following distances are based on typical stopping distances.

callouts.p: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
