core.p: Reaction time is the time between seeing a hazard and starting to act, for example moving your foot to the brake. During this time the car keeps moving at full speed.
bullets: Typical human reaction times are **0.2 s to 0.9 s**.
A typical value for an alert driver is about **0.7 s** for an emergency stop.
Reaction times vary from person to person and with conditions.
Thinking distance = speed × reaction time.
So doubling speed doubles thinking distance (thinking distance ∝ speed).

callouts.p: Reaction time: 0.2–0.9 s. Typical car speeds: about 13 m/s (30 mph) in towns and 31 m/s (70 mph) on motorways.

core.p: You can measure reaction times in a simple practical. The **ruler drop test** uses the distance a ruler falls before you catch it.
bullets: A partner holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark level with your open finger and thumb.
They drop it without warning; you catch it as fast as possible.
Read the distance fallen from the ruler at the top of your thumb.
Longer distance fallen means a **longer reaction time** (the ruler accelerates under gravity).
Convert distance to time with a conversion table or s = ½gt², so t = √(2s ÷ g).
Repeat several times and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of random errors.
Keep variables controlled: same hand, same starting gap, same person dropping.
Alternatively use a **computer reaction test** that times how quickly you click when a signal appears.

core.p: Anything that makes the driver react more slowly or makes the car move faster increases the thinking distance.
bullets: **Tiredness** increases reaction time.
**Alcohol** and **drugs** (including some medicines) increase reaction time.
**Distractions** such as using a mobile phone, loud music or passengers increase reaction time.
**Higher speed** means more distance is covered during the same reaction time.
Thinking distance is **not** affected by road conditions or the state of the brakes.

callouts.p: Wet or icy roads do not increase thinking distance; they increase braking distance.

core.p: Braking distance depends on how large the braking force can be and how much kinetic energy the car must lose.
bullets: **Speed**: braking distance increases a lot as speed increases.
**Mass** of the vehicle (passengers, luggage): more mass means more kinetic energy and a smaller deceleration for the same force.
**Road conditions**: wet, icy, oily or loose surfaces reduce friction between tyres and road.
**Tyres**: worn tyres with little tread grip less, especially on wet roads.
**Brakes**: worn or poorly maintained brakes give a smaller braking force.
Too large a braking force can make the wheels **skid**, which increases braking distance.

core.h: Speed and stopping distance on a graph
core.p: A velocity–time graph of an emergency stop shows the two parts of stopping distance clearly. The area under a velocity–time graph equals distance travelled.
bullets: During the reaction time the line is **flat** (constant velocity).
Area of the rectangle = thinking distance.
Once the brakes are applied the line slopes down (deceleration).
Area of the triangle = braking distance.
The gradient of the sloping part gives the deceleration.

core.p: When the brakes are applied, friction between the brake pads and the discs does **work** on the car. This transfers energy from the car's kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes.
bullets: Work done by brakes = braking force × braking distance.
Work done = kinetic energy lost = ½mv².
The brakes and discs **heat up**; very large braking can make them overheat and **fade**.
Kinetic energy ∝ v², so **doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy**.
For the same braking force, braking distance is therefore about **four times** as long at double speed.
Heavier vehicles need a larger braking force or a longer distance to stop.

callouts.p: Thinking distance ∝ speed, but braking distance ∝ speed². This is why stopping distances rise so steeply with speed.

core.p: Stopping very suddenly needs a very large force, because F = m × a. Large decelerations act on the car and on the people inside it.
bullets: A large deceleration needs a large resultant force on the body.
Large forces cause **serious injuries** (for example to the neck, chest and head) in a collision.
Large braking forces may cause the brakes to **overheat** or the car to **skid** and lose control.
Deceleration in a crash can be hundreds of m/s², many times that in normal braking.
Reducing the deceleration means increasing the **time** (or distance) over which the car or person stops.

core.h: Force, momentum and time in collisions
core.p: In a collision the change in momentum of a passenger is fixed by their mass and speed. Spreading this change over a longer time reduces the force.
bullets: Force = change in momentum ÷ time, F = Δ(mv) ÷ t.
For the same change in momentum, a **longer collision time** gives a **smaller force**.
This is equivalent to a **smaller deceleration**, since F = m × a.
A longer stopping distance during the collision also means less force, because work done F × d = kinetic energy lost.

callouts.p: Safety features increase the time taken to stop, so the rate of change of momentum (and the deceleration) is smaller, so the force on the person is smaller.

core.p: Modern cars are designed so that people inside slow down over a longer time and distance in a crash.
bullets: **Crumple zones**: front and rear of the car crumple, increasing the time taken for the car to stop.
**Seat belts**: stretch slightly, so the passenger slows down over a longer time; they also stop you hitting the windscreen.
**Air bags**: inflate and then deflate as you hit them, increasing the time to stop your head and spreading the force over a larger area.
**Collapsible steering columns** and **padded dashboards** also increase stopping time.
**Cycle and motorbike helmets** contain a crushable foam layer that increases the time for the head to stop.
**Crash barriers** and **gravel run-off areas** increase the stopping time and distance of vehicles.
**Anti-lock brakes (ABS)** prevent skidding so the driver can steer while braking.

head: Feature
How it reduces the force
rows: Stretches, so passenger stops over longer time
Longer time and larger area for the head
Foam crushes, head stops over longer time

core.p: Physics explains many road safety rules and advice, and exam questions often ask you to evaluate them.
bullets: Lower speed limits near schools cut both thinking and braking distance, and reduce collision forces.
The **two-second rule** keeps a gap larger than the thinking distance.
Drivers should **double** the gap on wet roads and allow up to **ten times** on icy roads.
Banning mobile phone use reduces distraction and reaction times.
Drink-drive limits exist because alcohol increases reaction time.

analogy.p: Stopping a car is like catching a fast cricket ball. Before your hands move you need to notice the ball (reaction time); the ball keeps flying towards you while you react (thinking distance). Then your hands slow the ball down (braking distance). Pulling your hands back as you catch spreads the stop over a longer time, so the ball stings less, just as a crumple zone or air bag reduces the force on a passenger. Where it breaks down: a car's braking force comes from friction between tyres and road, which depends on road conditions, and a car has far more kinetic energy, so its braking distance grows with the square of its speed.

terms.d: The total distance travelled from seeing a hazard to stopping: thinking distance + braking distance.
The distance travelled during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied.
The distance travelled after the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops.
The time between a stimulus (seeing a hazard) and the response (starting to brake); typically 0.2 to 0.9 s.
The friction force from the brakes and tyres that decelerates a vehicle.
A negative acceleration: the rate at which velocity decreases.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; needed between tyres and road for braking.
When the wheels lock and slide over the road, reducing control and often increasing braking distance.
Mass × velocity, measured in kg m/s.
A part of a car designed to deform in a collision, increasing the time to stop and reducing the force.
A restraint that stretches slightly to increase the time taken for a passenger to stop.
A bag that inflates in a crash to increase the stopping time of the head and spread the force over a larger area.
A method of measuring reaction time from the distance a dropped ruler falls before it is caught.
Loss of braking force when brakes overheat after being used hard.

mistakes.w: Icy roads increase thinking distance.
mistakes.r: Icy roads increase braking distance; thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed only.

mistakes.w: Alcohol increases braking distance.
mistakes.r: Alcohol increases reaction time and so thinking distance.

mistakes.w: Safety features reduce the change in momentum.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same; the time is longer, so the force (rate of change of momentum) is smaller.

mistakes.w: Crumple zones absorb the force.
mistakes.r: Crumple zones increase the time taken to stop, which reduces the deceleration and the force (they also transfer energy by deforming).

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles braking distance.
mistakes.r: Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, so braking distance is about four times longer for the same braking force.

mistakes.w: Stopping distance = thinking distance × braking distance.
mistakes.r: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

mistakes.w: Reaction time is about 5 s.
mistakes.r: Typical reaction time is 0.2 to 0.9 s.

mistakes.w: A longer ruler drop distance means quicker reactions.
mistakes.r: A longer distance fallen means a longer reaction time.

exam.q: State the equation that links stopping distance, thinking distance and braking distance.
model: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
exam.tip: Easy mark: learn it word for word.

exam.q: State a typical range of values for human reaction time.
model: 0.2 s to 0.9 s
exam.tip: Values in seconds, not minutes.

exam.q: Give two factors that increase thinking distance.
model: Any two from: greater speed / tiredness / alcohol / drugs / distractions such as a mobile phone
exam.tip: Do not give road conditions: they affect braking distance.

exam.q: Give two factors that increase braking distance, other than speed.
model: Any two from: wet or icy road / worn tyres / worn brakes / greater mass of vehicle / loose road surface
exam.tip: Be specific: 'bad weather' alone is too vague; say 'wet road'.

exam.q: A driver travelling at 20 m/s has a reaction time of 0.6 s. Calculate the thinking distance.
model: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 20 × 0.6
exam.tip: Speed is constant during the reaction time.

exam.q: Describe how to use a ruler to measure a person's reaction time and get a reliable result.
model: Partner holds ruler vertically, zero level with the open finger and thumb of the subject
Ruler dropped without warning; subject catches it; distance fallen read from ruler
Distance converted to reaction time using a table or s = ½gt²
Repeat several times and calculate a mean, keeping the same hand and starting position
exam.tip: Include repeats and controlled variables for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why braking distance increases more than thinking distance when speed doubles.
model: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time, so it doubles
Kinetic energy = ½mv², so doubling speed gives four times the kinetic energy
Work done by the (same) braking force = force × distance, so braking distance is four times as long
exam.tip: Link braking distance to kinetic energy and work done.

exam.q: Explain why braking hard for a long time from high speed can make the brakes less effective.
model: Work done by friction transfers kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes, so they get very hot
Overheated brakes give a smaller braking force (brake fade)
exam.tip: Mention energy transfer to thermal store.

exam.q: Explain why a large deceleration is dangerous for the occupants of a car.
model: A large deceleration needs a large force (F = ma)
Large forces on the body cause serious injury
exam.tip: Always link deceleration to force.

exam.q: Explain how a crumple zone reduces the risk of injury in a collision.
model: The crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop
The change in momentum is the same, so the rate of change of momentum / deceleration is smaller
So the force on the occupants is smaller
exam.tip: Say 'increases the time', then 'same change in momentum', then 'smaller force'.

exam.q: Discuss how the design of cars and the behaviour of drivers can improve road safety. Use ideas about stopping distance and forces in collisions.
model: Drivers should avoid alcohol, drugs, tiredness and distractions to keep reaction time and thinking distance short
Lower speeds reduce thinking distance (∝ speed) and braking distance (∝ speed²)
Keeping tyres and brakes in good condition and allowing larger gaps on wet or icy roads reduces braking distance
Crumple zones increase the time for the car to stop in a crash
Seat belts and air bags increase the time for the passenger to stop
Longer time means smaller rate of change of momentum, so smaller force and fewer injuries
exam.tip: Cover both avoiding a crash (stopping distance) and reducing injury in a crash (force and time).

worked.q: A car travels at 25 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.8 s. The braking distance is 48 m. Calculate the stopping distance.
steps: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time = 25 × 0.8 = 20 m
Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

worked.q: In a ruler drop test, the ruler falls 0.18 m before it is caught. Calculate the reaction time (g = 10 m/s²).
steps: The ruler starts from rest and accelerates at g, so s = ½gt²

worked.q: A 60 kg passenger travelling at 15 m/s is stopped by a seat belt in 0.20 s. Without a seat belt they hit the dashboard and stop in 0.02 s. Compare the forces.
steps: Change in momentum = m × Δv = 60 × 15 = 900 kg m/s
Same change in momentum, but 10 times longer time gives 10 times smaller force
worked.ans: 4500 N with the seat belt compared with 45 000 N without, ten times smaller
